title: Test Engineering (CEN315)
sourceNote: CEN315 Introduction to Test Engineering haftalık slaytlarından (Week 1–13) Claude tarafından üretildi. Şüpheli bir cevapta slayta bakın ve "Bu soruda sorun var" ile işaretleyin.

sets.title: Week 1: The Role of Test Engineering and Quality Fundamentals

prompt.en: How does the modern definition describe Test Engineering?

en: A process-auditing function that certifies teams against ISO standards
A developer-only practice limited to writing unit tests for each function
A distinct downstream phase that starts only once all coding is complete
A reactive QC activity performed after implementation, focused on finding defects
A proactive QA discipline across the whole lifecycle, aimed at preventing defects

explanation.en: The modern definition calls Test Engineering a proactive quality assurance discipline that spans the entire lifecycle and focuses on preventing defects; testing as a separate downstream phase describes the older waterfall role.

prompt.en: Which description matches Quality Assurance (QA)?

en: Checking the product's fitness for purpose together with stakeholders
Process-oriented activities such as policies, standards, audits and improvement loops
Product-oriented activities that evaluate whether a deliverable meets requirements
Checking the conformance of the product to its specifications
Dynamic evaluation of a product by executing it under specified conditions

explanation.en: QA is process-oriented and establishes confidence that quality will be achieved through policies, standards, audits and improvement loops; evaluating whether a specific deliverable meets requirements is Quality Control.

prompt.en: According to the course's definition of testing, what does testing provide?

en: Information about risk and quality, not guarantees
A guarantee that no defects remain in the product
Confidence that the development process will achieve quality
Formal proof that the product conforms to its specification
A complete record of every possible input and its output

explanation.en: Testing executes the product under specified conditions and observes outcomes, which provides information about risk and quality but no guarantees; building confidence in the process is what QA does.

prompt.en: Before release, a team lets real end users try the product to check whether it actually fits their needs and purpose. Which activity is this?

en: Static testing
Unit testing
Quality assurance audit
Validation
Verification

explanation.en: Validation asks 'Are we building the right product?' and checks fitness for purpose with stakeholders; verification only checks conformance to the specifications.

prompt.en: Which statement about Quality Assurance (QA) and Quality Control (QC) is correct?

en: QA is owned by QC personnel, while QC involves the entire organization
QA produces defect logs, while QC produces training materials
QA is proactive/preventive, while QC is reactive/detective
QA is product-oriented, while QC is process-oriented
QA is reactive/detective, while QC is proactive/preventive

explanation.en: The QA/QC comparison lists QA as proactive/preventive and process-oriented (the whole team's responsibility) and QC as reactive/detective and product-oriented (done by QC personnel).

prompt.en: In the ISO/IEC 25010 product quality model, testability is listed as a sub-characteristic of which characteristic?

en: Reliability
Functional suitability
Usability
Portability
Maintainability

explanation.en: ISO/IEC 25010 lists testability under Maintainability, together with modularity, reusability, analyzability and modifiability.

prompt.en: Which of the following is a static testing activity?

en: Executing unit tests in the CI pipeline
Conducting user acceptance testing (UAT)
Running API/integration tests against a service
Running a linter and SAST on the source code
Running a performance test on the system

explanation.en: Static testing evaluates artefacts without executing the code, and linters and SAST are listed static examples; unit, performance, UAT and API/integration tests execute the system, so they are dynamic.

prompt.en: What is the core idea of Equivalence Partitioning (EP)?

en: Group inputs into classes that behave alike and test one representative per class
Test the minimum, maximum and the values just inside and outside each limit
Execute every possible input value to reach complete input coverage
Rank test items by likelihood, impact and detectability before testing them
Enumerate combinations of conditions and the expected outcome of each one

explanation.en: EP partitions inputs into classes expected to behave similarly and tests one representative from each class; testing the minimum, maximum and their neighbours is boundary value analysis.

prompt.en: Which test design technique is meant for logic with multiple conditions, enumerating their combinations and expected outcomes?

en: Risk-based testing
Decision tables / cause-effect
Boundary value analysis
Exploratory testing
Equivalence partitioning

explanation.en: Decision tables / cause-effect handle logic with multiple conditions by enumerating condition combinations and expected outcomes, minimized with pairwise where appropriate.

prompt.en: A password must be 8–20 characters long. Which set of length equivalence classes matches the course's worked example?

en: <7 invalid, 7–21 valid, >21 invalid
<8 invalid, 8–20 invalid, >20 valid
<8 invalid, 8–20 valid, >20 invalid
<8 valid, 8–20 valid, >20 invalid
<8 invalid, 8–20 valid, >20 valid

explanation.en: The worked example partitions length into <8 (invalid), 8–20 (valid) and >20 (invalid); 7 and 21 are boundary test values, not limits of the valid class.

prompt.en: An input field accepts integers from 1 to 100. Testing just below, at and just above each boundary, which values does boundary value analysis select?

explanation.en: BVA tests just below, at and just above each boundary: 0, 1, 2 around the minimum and 99, 100, 101 around the maximum; leaving out 2 and 99 misses the just-inside values.

prompt.en: Using the course's risk-based testing rubric, a feature is rated likelihood 4, impact 5 and detectability 2. What is its RPN?

explanation.en: RPN = Likelihood × Impact × Detectability = 4 × 5 × 2 = 40; 20 ignores detectability and 11 adds the scores instead of multiplying them.

prompt.en: On the 1–5 risk-based testing rubric, what does a detectability score of 5 mean?

en: Frequent in the field or code-change area
Hard to detect until production
Safety, financial or regulatory breach
Cosmetic impact only
Easy to detect before release

explanation.en: On the rubric, detectability 1 means easy to detect pre-release and 5 means hard to detect until production, so a higher detectability score raises the risk.

prompt.en: In the risk assessment matrix, what risk level results from a Remote (D) probability combined with Catastrophic (1) severity?

en: Eliminated
Low
High
Medium
Serious

explanation.en: In the matrix, Remote (D) with Catastrophic (1) is rated Serious; Catastrophic severity becomes High only at Occasional (C) or a more frequent probability.

prompt.en: How does the test engineer's role differ between sequential (waterfall) and incremental development?

en: Waterfall: testing is a distinct downstream phase; incremental: testers take part repeatedly across increments
Waterfall: testers sit in cross-functional teams; incremental: testing starts after deployment
Waterfall: testers take part repeatedly across increments; incremental: testing is a distinct downstream phase
Waterfall: early feedback becomes possible; incremental: feedback waits until deployment
Waterfall: regression testing is central; incremental: regression testing is no longer needed

explanation.en: In waterfall, testing is a distinct downstream phase; in incremental development, software is developed and tested in increments, so testers participate repeatedly, regression testing becomes important and early feedback is possible.

prompt.en: How does the test engineer's position change in Agile and DevOps environments?

en: Test engineers form a separate team that tests after implementation
Test engineers focus on manual testing and avoid test automation
Test engineers join the project only during the maintenance phase
Test engineers test only once the full release has been completed
Test engineers become integrated members of cross-functional teams

explanation.en: With CI/CD, continuous testing, test automation and shift-left testing, test engineers in Agile and DevOps become integrated members of cross-functional teams rather than a separate downstream group.

prompt.en: Which responsibility is listed under a modern test engineer's Quality Assurance focus?

en: Establishing quality gates and exit criteria
Reviewing overnight CI/CD test results
Conducting exploratory testing sessions
Developing test automation frameworks
Managing test data and test environments

explanation.en: Establishing quality gates and exit criteria is listed under the Quality Assurance focus; reviewing overnight CI/CD results is a daily activity, while automation frameworks, exploratory testing and test data/environments are technical activities.

prompt.en: In the testing pyramid, which description fits the base layer?

en: Unit tests: fewer tests, slower execution, higher cost
Unit tests: many tests, fast execution, low cost
Integration tests: moderate number, medium speed and cost
System/E2E tests: many tests, fast execution, low cost
System/E2E tests: fewer tests, slower execution, higher cost

explanation.en: The base of the pyramid is unit tests: many tests, fast execution and low cost; fewer, slower and costlier tests belong to the System/E2E top, and integration tests sit in the middle.

prompt.en: Which statement correctly describes unit testing?

en: Done on the complete integrated application across browsers
Done by an independent test team in a production-like environment
Done by developers, mostly white-box, with mocked dependencies
Done by external users in their own real environment
Done by business users to validate the business requirements

explanation.en: Unit testing is performed by developers, primarily white-box, in a development environment with mocked dependencies; an independent team in a production-like environment describes system testing.

prompt.en: A team integrates the low-level modules first and writes drivers to call them. Which integration strategy is this?

en: Top-down
Big Bang
Sandwich/Hybrid
Bottom-up
System integration

explanation.en: Bottom-up integration starts with low-level modules and uses drivers; top-down starts with top-level modules and uses stubs, and Big Bang integrates all modules simultaneously.

prompt.en: During system testing, a tester runs the application on several browsers and operating systems. Which type of system testing is this?

en: Compatibility testing
Performance testing
Security testing
Usability testing
Functional testing

explanation.en: Compatibility testing covers different browsers and operating systems; performance covers response times, throughput and scalability, and usability covers user experience and interface design.

prompt.en: What distinguishes beta testing from alpha testing?

en: Beta is done by an independent test team; alpha is done by external end users
Beta uses external users in a real environment; alpha is internal testing by the organization
Beta is the final validation by business users; alpha is unit testing by developers
Beta tests interactions between modules; alpha tests the complete integrated system
Beta is internal testing by the organization; alpha uses external users in a real environment

explanation.en: Alpha testing is internal testing by the organization, while beta testing uses external users in a real environment; final validation by business users is User Acceptance Testing (UAT).

prompt.en: According to the course's ethics guidance, how should test engineers handle Personally Identifiable Information (PII) in test data?

en: Copy unmodified production data for realism
Keep PII unmasked but only in test environments
Include real PII in reports for traceability
Avoid documenting assumptions about the data
Use masked or synthetic data where possible

explanation.en: The ethics guidance says to respect privacy and PII by using masked or synthetic data where possible, and to document residual risk and assumptions explicitly.

prompt.en: In the V-model diagram, which testing level is paired with Requirement Gathering on the opposite side of the V?

en: Static Testing
Integration Testing
Unit Testing
System Testing
Acceptance Testing

explanation.en: In the V-model, Requirement Gathering is paired with Acceptance Testing; System Analysis pairs with System Testing, Software Design with Integration Testing and Module Design with Unit Testing.

prompt.en: Which question summarizes verification?

en: Does the test look at the code?
Are we building the product right?
Is the test based on spec or on use?
Are we building the right product?
Does the test execute the code?

explanation.en: Verification asks 'Are we building the product right?' and checks conformance to specs; 'Are we building the right product?' is validation, which checks fitness for purpose with stakeholders.

prompt.en: In the V-lifecycle testing diagram, which pairing of testing approach and lifecycle levels is shown?

en: White-box — Specification and SW Integration
White-box — Analysis and System Test
Black-box — Specification and SW Integration
Random test — Design and Unit Test
White-box — Analysis and Specification

explanation.en: The V-lifecycle diagram groups Specification and SW Integration as black-box, Design, Implementation and Unit Test as white-box, and Analysis and System Test as random test.

prompt.en: What characterizes black-box testing?

en: The code is evaluated without the program being executed
Each individual unit is tested in isolation by its developer
The tester knows the internal structure and code of the software
The internal structure and code are hidden; nothing is known about them
Test inputs are chosen at random instead of from a specification

explanation.en: In black-box testing the internal structure, program or code is hidden and nothing is known about it; knowing the internal structure is white-box testing.

prompt.en: A tester reads a method's source code, designs inputs to reach each branch, and then runs those tests. How is this testing classified?

en: Dynamic and white-box
Dynamic and black-box
Random and black-box
Static and black-box
Static and white-box

explanation.en: Running the tests executes the code, so it is dynamic, and designing them from the source code means the tester looks at the code, so it is white-box.

prompt.en: What problem are unit testing frameworks such as JUnit and NUnit meant to address?

en: GUI tests cannot be automated, so every user journey must be checked by hand
Production code cannot be compiled until a full system test has been run
Developers cannot deploy to production without an independent test team
Testing is not closely integrated with development, so progress cannot be measured
Requirements cannot be reviewed with stakeholders before coding starts

explanation.en: JUnit/NUnit address the problem that testing is not closely integrated with development, which prevents measuring progress; their philosophy is to develop tests in parallel with the application code or before it.

prompt.en: Which statement matches the testing percentages recommended in the course?

en: Unit tests verify class interactions and make up 20% of tests
System tests verify class interactions and make up 20% of tests
Unit tests verify end-to-end journeys and make up 10% of tests
GUI tests verify end-to-end journeys and make up 70% of tests
System tests verify a single class and make up 70% of tests

explanation.en: The slide gives unit tests (behavior of a single class) 70%, system tests (class interactions) 20% and GUI tests (end-to-end journeys) 10% of all tests.

prompt.en: In the test pyramid diagram, what changes as you move up from unit tests toward UI and manual tests?

en: More integration and slower tests
More isolation but slower tests
More integration but faster tests
More tests and a lower cost per test
More isolation and faster tests

explanation.en: The pyramid's arrows point to more integration and slower tests toward the top (UI and manual tests), and to more isolation and faster tests toward unit tests at the base.

prompt.en: Which statement matches the Units diagram that compares E2E, service and unit scopes?

en: The service scope covers the user interface and all microservices
The E2E scope covers only one Func() and its database
A unit spans the user interface and several microservices
A unit must always include the service's database
A unit is one Func() or a small group of Func()s in a service

explanation.en: The diagram shows one Unit bracket around a single Func() and another around a small group of Func()s inside the service; the E2E scope is the one that spans the user interface and the microservices.

prompt.en: In the TestNG CalculatorTest class, what does the @BeforeMethod-annotated setUp() method do?

en: Asserts that the Calculator constructor throws no errors
Runs as an extra test that must pass before testAdd()
Creates a new Calculator before each test method runs
Creates one Calculator after all test methods finish
Resets the test results after each failed assertion

explanation.en: The @BeforeMethod setUp() runs before each test method and assigns a new Calculator, so every test starts with a fresh object; it is setup code, not a test itself.

prompt.en: Calculator.add returns a + b and subtract returns a - b. CalculatorTest asserts that add(5, 3) equals 8 and subtract(5, 3) equals 2. What does the TestNG run report?

en: Tests run: 2, Failures: 0, Skips: 1
Tests run: 2, Failures: 0, Skips: 0
Tests run: 3, Failures: 0, Skips: 0
Tests run: 1, Failures: 0, Skips: 0
Tests run: 2, Failures: 1, Skips: 0

explanation.en: Both @Test methods, testAdd and testSubtract, pass because add and subtract are implemented correctly, so TestNG reports 2 tests run with 0 failures and 0 skips; setUp() is not counted as a test.

prompt.en: What is the role of assertions in a unit test?

en: They call the method under test with the inputs prepared for the test
They replace slow dependencies so that the unit can run in isolation
They create the objects and input values that the test needs before it runs
They record how long each test method takes to finish executing
They express requirements the unit must meet, replacing human checking

explanation.en: Assertions ensure the code behaves as expected: they express the requirements the unit under test must meet and replace humans in checking that the software does what it should; creating objects is Arrange and calling the method is Act.

prompt.en: In the C# BankTests project (Microsoft.VisualStudio.TestTools.UnitTesting), which attributes mark the test class and a test method?

en: [UnitTest] and [TestMethod]
@BeforeMethod and @Test
[TestClass] and [Test]
[TestClass] and [TestMethod]
[TestSuite] and [TestCase]

explanation.en: The BankAccountTests class is marked [TestClass] and its test methods [TestMethod]; @BeforeMethod and @Test are the TestNG annotations from the Java example.

prompt.en: In the Debit_WithValidAmount_UpdatesBalance test, what happens in the Arrange section?

en: The starting values and the BankAccount under test are set up
The actual balance is compared with the expected value 7.44
account.Debit(debitAmount) is called on the account object
The intentionally incorrect Debit code is corrected first
The class is marked with [TestClass] so that it can run

explanation.en: Arrange sets beginningBalance, debitAmount and expected and creates the BankAccount; calling Debit is the Act step and comparing actual with expected is the Assert step.

prompt.en: The BankAccount.Debit method contains intentionally incorrect code. Which change fixes it so that the debit test passes?

en: Replace m_balance -= amount with m_balance += amount
Make m_balance a readonly field like m_customerName
Replace m_balance += amount with m_balance -= amount
Replace amount > m_balance with amount < m_balance
Remove the check that throws when amount < 0

explanation.en: Debit wrongly adds the amount to the balance (m_balance += amount, marked as intentionally incorrect); the fix replaces it with m_balance -= amount, after which the test passes.

prompt.en: Which of the following is listed as a benefit of unit testing?

en: No ongoing maintenance of test cases
Full coverage of interactions between units
Facilitation of refactoring
Thorough testing of user interfaces
Independence from the developers

explanation.en: Facilitation of refactoring is one of the seven listed benefits; maintenance overhead, dependence on developers, and difficulty testing user interfaces and interactions are listed as disadvantages.

prompt.en: Why is over-reliance on automated unit tests listed as a disadvantage?

en: Automated unit tests can only check the user interface
Automated unit tests cannot run inside a CI/CD pipeline
Automation makes ongoing test maintenance unnecessary
Automated unit tests always run slower than manual tests
It can create a false sense of security about remaining bugs

explanation.en: Over-reliance on automation can lead to a false sense of security, because automated tests may not uncover all possible issues or bugs.

prompt.en: A project relies only on unit tests, and later bugs appear in how two modules exchange data. Which disadvantage of unit testing does this illustrate?

en: Time and effort
Difficulty in testing interactions
Difficulty in testing user interfaces
Maintenance overhead
Dependence on developers

explanation.en: Unit testing focuses only on individual units, so it may not be sufficient for testing interactions between units.

prompt.en: A developer writes the unit tests for a new feature before writing the feature's code. Which practice is this?

en: Manual unit testing
Continuous delivery
Static testing
Test-Driven Development (TDD)
Black-box system testing

explanation.en: In Test-Driven Development, developers write tests before writing the actual code; manual unit testing means checking each part by hand without special tools.

prompt.en: In the example CI/CD setup, a Git user pushes code to a GitHub repository that contains unit tests. What happens next?

en: A Git webhook triggers AWS CodeBuild, so the unit tests run automatically
The repository waits for the weekly scheduled test run to start
The unit tests run only after the code is deployed to production
A tester manually runs the unit tests before the next release date
AWS CodeBuild sends the code back to the user for a manual review

explanation.en: The push to the repository fires a Git webhook to AWS CodeBuild; in CI/CD, unit tests run automatically whenever new code is added instead of being run by hand.

prompt.en: Why is manual unit testing not used much, according to the course?

en: Developers are not allowed to test their own code by hand
It requires special testing tools that developers do not have
It costs more and must be repeated every time the code changes
It can only start after the system has been deployed
It can only be applied to graphical user interfaces

explanation.en: Manual unit testing costs more because people are paid for their testing time and takes a lot of time because tests must be redone whenever the code changes; it needs no special tools and developers often do it themselves.

prompt.en: In the CI/CD pipeline diagram, which step comes immediately before deploying changes to production?

en: Run the tests
Deliver the build to staging
Notify the build outcome
Notify the test outcome
Trigger the build

explanation.en: The pipeline order is Commit, Trigger, Build, Notify build outcome, Run tests, Notify test outcome, Deliver build to staging, then Deploy changes to production.

prompt.en: Which set of characteristics describes a unit test?

en: Tests one function or class in isolation; fast and deterministic
Tests one function but may give different results on each run
Tests the full user journey through the UI on a staging system
Tests one class against a real database so results match production
Tests several services together through their real network APIs

explanation.en: A unit test validates a single unit (function/class) in isolation with fast, deterministic, repeatable checks. Spanning services, the UI or a real database breaks isolation, and changing results contradict "deterministic".

prompt.en: In the Red → Green → Refactor cycle of TDD, what is done in the green step?

en: Clean up the design while using the tests as a safety net
Write a failing test that specifies the next behavior
Write the complete design of the module before any code
Add tests for code that has already been fully implemented
Write the minimal code needed to make the failing test pass

explanation.en: Green means making the failing test pass with minimal code. Writing the failing test first is the red step, and cleaning up with the tests as a safety net is the refactor step.

prompt.en: In the step-by-step TDD workflow, how long should each cycle typically be kept?

en: About 1–2 hours
About one working day
About 2–10 minutes
About one full sprint
Under 1 second

explanation.en: The workflow says to repeat and keep cycles short (2–10 min) to maintain momentum. Under 1 second is the target for running a local test suite segment, not for a TDD cycle.

prompt.en: Which statement about TDD is correct?

en: It requires a complete, detailed design to be made up front
It is a form of end-to-end testing through the user interface
It means writing the unit tests after the code is finished
It complements, rather than replaces, integration and E2E tests
It works best with large units that are entangled with I/O

explanation.en: TDD is not writing tests after coding, not full design up front and not end-to-end testing; it complements higher-level tests. Large units entangled with I/O are listed as a pitfall because they slow the cycles.

prompt.en: In the comparison of Big Design Up Front and Emergent Design, which characteristic belongs to Emergent Design?

en: Fixes the design before coding
Assumes change is cheap
Think before you code
Requires abstract thinking
Supports governance

explanation.en: Emergent Design assumes change is cheap, handles ambiguity and requires detail thinking. Thinking before you code, supporting governance and requiring abstract thinking are listed for Big Design Up Front.

prompt.en: Among the limits and pitfalls of TDD, what does "test theater" mean?

en: Tests that run slowly because the units are too large
Tests that mock every collaborator and become fragile
Tests that fail randomly because of time or concurrency
Tests that produce coverage without adding real value
Tests that break because they over-specify internals

explanation.en: "Test theater" is listed as coverage without value. Over-specifying internals, mocking everything and overly large units are separate pitfalls, and random failures from time or concurrency describe flaky tests.

prompt.en: A class reads its configuration from a global static singleton, which makes it hard to unit test. Which change follows the design-for-testability guidance?

en: Inject the dependency through an interface or abstraction
Test it only end-to-end so the real singleton gets set up
Move the configuration into another global static variable
Merge the class and its dependencies into one larger unit
Make the singleton's fields public so tests can change them

explanation.en: Designing for testability favors dependency inversion with interfaces/abstractions and clear seams for substituting dependencies, and says to avoid global state and static singletons that hide dependencies.

prompt.en: A constructor requires a logger parameter, but the behavior under test never uses the logger. Which type of test double is intended for this case?

en: Fake
Spy
Stub
Mock
Dummy

explanation.en: A dummy is passed but never used. Stubs return canned values, fakes are lightweight working implementations, spies record interactions and mocks verify them, none of which is needed here.

prompt.en: What distinguishes a mock from a stub?

en: A mock is a working in-memory version; a stub is never used
A mock is passed but never used; a stub records interactions
A mock verifies interactions; a stub returns canned values
A mock records interactions only; a stub verifies call arguments
A mock returns canned values; a stub verifies interactions

explanation.en: A mock verifies behavior/interaction while a stub returns canned values. Being passed but never used describes a dummy, a lightweight working implementation is a fake, and recording interactions is a spy.

prompt.en: Which dependency is the most appropriate to mock in a unit test?

en: The system under test whose behavior is checked
An external HTTP service that the class calls
The project's own domain data model classes
The sorting algorithm the team implemented
A simple value object defined in the codebase

explanation.en: Mocking is recommended for external or hard-to-control dependencies such as I/O, time and HTTP. The course says not to mock your own data models or algorithms, and the system under test is exercised, not replaced.

prompt.en: When using a mocking framework, why should mocks be reset or torn down between tests?

en: To raise the statement and branch coverage of the suite
To verify how many times each method was called
To stub exceptions thrown by the mocked dependency
To keep state from leaking from one test into the next
To set up given/when expectations for the next call

explanation.en: Resetting/teardown isolates state between tests to avoid leakage. Verifying call counts, stubbing exceptions and arranging given/when expectations are separate mocking-framework patterns.

prompt.en: In the Arrange–Act–Assert structure, what belongs to the Act phase?

en: Invoking exactly one behavior of the system under test
Resetting mocks so that no state leaks into later tests
Invoking several behaviors in a row to share one setup
Checking the resulting outcome or the interaction made
Creating the inputs, test doubles and system under test

explanation.en: Act invokes one behavior; preparing inputs, doubles and the system under test is Arrange, and checking the outcome or interaction is Assert. Invoking several behaviors contradicts the one-behavior-per-test rule.

prompt.en: You want to run the same test logic against many input values, including boundary values and representatives of each equivalence class, without copying the test. Which technique fits?

en: Spies that record every interaction
Parameterized tests driven by data sets
Smoke tests after promotion to staging
Mutation testing of the assertions
A canary rollout with gradual traffic

explanation.en: Parameterized tests cover multiple cases with data sets and focus on boundary values and equivalence classes. Mutation testing measures how strong the tests are rather than adding input cases.

prompt.en: A unit test fails intermittently because it uses the current system time and unseeded random numbers. Which fix matches the recommended approach?

en: Raise the minimum coverage threshold in the pipeline
Run the test concurrently with others to expose timing
Control the clock and seed the random number generator
Move the test into the nightly end-to-end test suite
Read the time from a real network time server instead

explanation.en: Flakiness caused by time and randomness is fixed by controlling clocks and RNGs (seeds/clocks). Real networks and concurrency are themselves listed as causes of flaky tests, not fixes.

prompt.en: Weak assertions can still yield high coverage. Which technique is suggested to catch such weak assertions?

en: Branch coverage
Build matrices
Smoke testing
Contract testing
Mutation testing

explanation.en: Statement/branch/condition coverage is useful but not a goal, because weak assertions can still produce high coverage; mutation testing is named as the way to catch weak assertions.

prompt.en: Which of the following is listed as a test smell or anti-pattern?

en: Arranging inputs and doubles before acting
Slow "unit" tests that touch real I/O
Seeding randomness to keep tests deterministic
Using fakes to keep tests realistic and fast
One behavior per test with a clear name

explanation.en: Slow "unit" tests touching real I/O are listed as a smell alongside over-mocking, testing private internals and giant copy-pasted setups. The other options are practices the course recommends.

prompt.en: As a reason to automate testing, what does "shift-left" mean?

en: Moving most testing to just before the production release
Replacing most unit tests with a larger set of E2E tests
Waiting to automate tests until the code is fully stable
Running the test suite only in the production environment
Catching issues earlier in the development process

explanation.en: Automation catches issues early, which is what "shift-left" means. Pushing testing toward release or production is the opposite, and replacing unit tests with E2E tests contradicts the testing pyramid.

prompt.en: A team has 400 end-to-end tests, 60 integration tests and 20 unit tests, and feedback is slow. What does the testing pyramid suggest?

en: Keep equal numbers of unit, integration and E2E tests
Replace the unit tests with integration tests against services
Have many fast unit tests, fewer integration and few E2E tests
Remove all E2E tests and rely on unit tests alone
Add more E2E tests, since they give the broadest confidence

explanation.en: The pyramid calls for many fast, cheap unit tests, fewer service/integration tests and few end-to-end tests to keep feedback quick. Integration/E2E tests are still used for cross-service confidence, so removing them all is wrong.

prompt.en: After a trigger such as a push or PR, which order matches the high-level pipeline anatomy?

en: Build → Test → Analyze → Package → Deploy
Build → Package → Deploy → Test → Analyze
Analyze → Build → Deploy → Package → Test
Build → Analyze → Deploy → Test → Package
Test → Build → Package → Analyze → Deploy

explanation.en: A pipeline triggers on push/PR/schedule, then runs Build → Test → Analyze → Package → Deploy, followed by feedback such as status checks, artifacts and notifications.

prompt.en: Which activity belongs to the typical CD stages rather than the typical CI stages?

en: Integration tests with services such as a DB or API
Unit tests run in parallel or as a matrix
Checkout and dependency restore with caching
Smoke tests and health checks on staging
Linting and static analysis such as SAST

explanation.en: CD promotes the build to staging, runs smoke tests and health checks, and gates promotion to production. Checkout, dependency caching, linting/static analysis, unit tests and integration tests are listed as CI stages.

prompt.en: How does trunk-based development compare with GitFlow?

en: Both offer identical trade-offs, so choosing between them does not matter
Both remove the need for PR checks as quality gates before merging
Both are production deployment strategies, like canary and blue/green
Trunk-based offers stricter release control; GitFlow enables rapid integration
Trunk-based enables rapid integration; GitFlow offers stricter release control

explanation.en: Trunk-based development enables rapid integration while GitFlow offers stricter release control. They are branching models with trade-offs, not deployment strategies, and PR checks are still used as quality gates.

prompt.en: Which pairing of acronym and pipeline topic is correct?

en: SBOM – deployment strategy
SAST – artifact versioning
SLSA – provenance of builds
AAA – pipeline triggers
SemVer – secrets scanning

explanation.en: SLSA basics are named together with build provenance. SemVer is for versioned artifacts, SBOM belongs to dependency scanning, SAST to static analysis/security checks, and AAA (Arrange–Act–Assert) to unit test structure.

prompt.en: Which pairing of test type and typical CI timing is correct?

en: Fast unit tests – only nightly, never on push
E2E/UI tests – on every push before linting
Performance and load tests – on every single push
Performance and load tests – on a schedule or pre-release
Contract/integration tests – only after production deploy

explanation.en: Fast unit tests run on every push, contract/integration tests on PRs or nightly, E2E/UI tests on staging or nightly, and performance/load tests on a schedule or pre-release to balance speed and depth.

prompt.en: Which description of a deployment strategy is correct?

en: Rolling: updates instances in batches with health checks
Feature flags: tie each deployment directly to a release
Blue/green: gradual rollout driven by production metrics
Canary: switches all traffic instantly with easy rollback
Rolling: updates all instances at once without any checks

explanation.en: Rolling updates change instances in batches with health checks. Blue/green gives an instant switch and easy rollback, canary is a gradual metrics-driven rollout, and feature flags decouple deploy from release.

prompt.en: Which duration do the team best practices target for PR pipelines?

en: Under about 1 hour
Under about 10 minutes
Under about 24 hours
Under about 1 second
Under about 4 hours

explanation.en: Best practices say to keep PR pipelines under about 10 minutes and to fail fast with clear, actionable messages. Under 1 second is the target for a local test suite segment, not a whole pipeline.

sets.title: Week 4: Coverage Metrics and Mutation Testing

prompt.en: Why is code coverage described as a white-box metric?

en: Measuring it requires access to the program's source code
It can be measured without running the test suite at all
It is computed from the number of faults the tests detect
It checks whether each test verifies the expected results
It is measured only from the program's inputs and outputs

explanation.en: Code coverage quantifies how much of the source code is executed when the test suite runs, so measuring it requires the source code. It does not check whether results are verified or count detected faults.

prompt.en: A test suite executes every statement of a module but contains no assertions. What does the lecture say about such a suite?

en: It kills most mutants, but its coverage cannot be measured
It can reach 100% statement coverage but kills almost no mutants
It reaches 0% statement coverage because nothing is verified
It can reach 100% statement coverage and kills most mutants
Its statement coverage is capped at 50% until assertions exist

explanation.en: Coverage shows what was executed, not what was verified, so an assertion-free suite can still reach 100%. Because nothing checks the output, it kills almost no mutants (only those that crash or hang).

prompt.en: Consider the code if (x > 0) { y = 1; } with no else. A single test with x = 5 is run. What coverage does this test achieve for the code?

en: 50% statement coverage and 100% branch coverage
100% statement coverage and 100% branch coverage
50% statement coverage and 50% branch coverage
100% statement coverage and 0% branch coverage
100% statement coverage and 50% branch coverage

explanation.en: The true outcome executes every statement, but an if without an else has two outcomes and the false outcome is never taken, so only 1 of 2 branch outcomes (50%) is covered.

prompt.en: A class has 8 methods. The tests call 6 of them, and one of the called methods contains an if body that no test executes. What is the function coverage?

explanation.en: Function coverage = functions called / total functions × 100 = 6 / 8 × 100 = 75%. Untested code inside a called method does not lower it, which is why function coverage is the weakest criterion.

prompt.en: For the decision if (A || B || C), assume all three conditions are evaluated in every test (no short-circuit evaluation). Across all tests A takes both true and false, B is only ever true, and C is only ever false. What is the condition coverage?

explanation.en: Condition coverage = condition outcomes exercised / (2 × number of conditions) × 100 = 4 / (2 × 3) × 100 ≈ 66.7%. The four exercised outcomes are A true, A false, B true and C false.

prompt.en: For if (A && B), with no short-circuit evaluation, the only tests are (A = true, B = false) and (A = false, B = true). Which result is correct?

en: Condition coverage is 100% and branch coverage is 50%
Condition coverage is 100% and branch coverage is 100%
Condition coverage is 50% and branch coverage is 100%
Condition coverage is 100% and branch coverage is 0%
Condition coverage is 50% and branch coverage is 50%

explanation.en: A and B each take both values, so condition coverage is 100%, but A && B is false in both tests, so the if body never runs and only the false outcome is covered (50%). This is why 100% condition coverage does not guarantee 100% branch coverage.

prompt.en: When can line coverage and statement coverage give different results for the same tests?

en: When a decision contains more than one Boolean condition
When the tests execute the code but contain no assertions
When some paths through the function are infeasible
When the same function is called by more than one test
When a single line contains more than one statement

explanation.en: Line coverage counts executable lines and statement coverage counts statements, so they differ when one line holds several statements, e.g. if (x > 0) y = 1;. Several conditions in one decision is what separates condition coverage from branch coverage instead.

prompt.en: A loop processes a list and can run at most 10 times (max = 10). Following the loop coverage guidance, which iteration counts should the tests use?

en: 0, 5 and 10 iterations only, as equal partitions
1, multiple, 10 and 11 iterations, but never 0
Only 10 and 11 iterations, to check the limit
0, 1, multiple, 9 and 10 iterations, and try 11
0 and 1 iterations only; multiple is optional

explanation.en: Loop coverage requires zero, one and multiple iterations; with a known maximum you also test max − 1 and max and try max + 1, because off-by-one errors often hide at these boundaries.

en: Statement, branch and condition coverage
Statement and branch coverage, but not condition coverage
Statement coverage only; branch coverage stays below 100%
Condition coverage, but not statement or branch coverage
Branch coverage only; statement coverage stays below 100%

explanation.en: T1 makes the first decision true and the second false, T2 does the opposite, so every statement and all four branch outcomes are executed. The condition y > 0 is never false (in T2, x > 0 is already false so y > 0 is not even evaluated, and y = 5 would be true anyway), so condition coverage stays below 100% until a test such as T3 = (1, −1) is added.

prompt.en: A function executes if (x > 0 && y > 0) r = 1; followed by if (x == 0) r = -1; and then returns r. Treating each if statement as one two-way decision, how many entry-to-exit paths does it have, and how many are feasible?

en: 2 paths, and both are feasible
3 paths, and all 3 are feasible
4 paths, of which 3 are feasible
4 paths, and all 4 are feasible
8 paths, of which 6 are feasible

explanation.en: Two independent if statements create 2^2 = 4 paths, but the path that makes both decisions true needs x > 0 and x == 0 at the same time, so no input can execute it (an infeasible path).

prompt.en: What does it mean that coverage criterion A subsumes criterion B?

en: No test set that satisfies A can also satisfy B
A and B always need the same number of test cases
Every test set that satisfies B also satisfies A
Every test set that satisfies A also satisfies B
A and B count the same items with different formulas

explanation.en: A subsumes B if every test set that satisfies A also satisfies B; the subsuming criterion is stronger, needs more tests and gives more confidence. The reversed direction is the most common mistake.

prompt.en: Which statement about the relationship between coverage criteria is true?

en: Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage, but not vice versa
Condition coverage subsumes branch coverage
A stronger criterion needs fewer tests and gives more confidence
Branch coverage subsumes condition coverage
Statement coverage subsumes branch coverage, but not vice versa

explanation.en: Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage, but not the other way round, and condition coverage and branch coverage do not subsume each other. A stronger criterion needs more tests, not fewer.

prompt.en: Each test below is written as (A, B). Which test set satisfies MC/DC for the decision if (A && B)?

en: (true, true), (false, true)
(false, false), (true, false), (false, true)
(true, true), (false, true), (true, false)
(true, false), (false, true)
(true, true), (false, false)

explanation.en: Going from (true, true) to (false, true) changes only A and flips the outcome, and going to (true, false) changes only B and flips it, so each condition is shown to independently affect the decision. The set (true, false), (false, true) never makes the decision true.

prompt.en: For a decision with 4 conditions, MC/DC can often be achieved with how many tests, compared with the number needed to try every combination?

en: 5 tests instead of 8
8 tests instead of 16
4 tests instead of 8
4 tests instead of 16
5 tests instead of 16

explanation.en: MC/DC can often be achieved with n + 1 = 5 tests, while trying every combination needs 2^n = 2^4 = 16 tests. MC/DC is required for the most safety-critical avionics software (DO-178C, Level A).

prompt.en: Which pairing of tool and purpose is correct?

en: Stryker: code coverage for JavaScript
PIT (Pitest): mutation testing for Java
Codecov: measuring code coverage for Java
mutmut: code coverage for Python
JaCoCo: mutation testing for Java

explanation.en: PIT is the Java mutation testing tool. JaCoCo measures Java code coverage, Stryker and mutmut are mutation testing tools, and Codecov only collects and displays reports from other tools without measuring coverage itself.

prompt.en: Which of the following is an advantage of measuring code coverage?

en: It shows whether each test checks its results
It exposes dead or unreachable code
It makes 100% path coverage practical for most code
It detects requirements that were never implemented
It directly measures the fault-detection ability of tests

explanation.en: Coverage reveals code that no test executes, including dead or unreachable code. It cannot detect missing code or show whether results were checked, and directly measuring fault-detection ability is an advantage of mutation testing.

prompt.en: A requirement was never implemented, yet the test suite reaches 100% statement coverage. Why does coverage not reveal this fault?

en: There is no code for the requirement, so nothing exists to cover
The fault is an equivalent mutant, so no test can detect it
Coverage tools skip code that no assertion checks
The missing code lies on an infeasible path, so it is excluded
Statement coverage counts only functions, not statements

explanation.en: Coverage cannot detect missing code (faults of omission): if a requirement was never implemented, there is no code to cover, so the metric can be 100% while the feature is missing.

prompt.en: When code coverage becomes a target, developers may write shallow tests just to raise the number. What does the lecture call this effect?

en: Infeasible paths
Faults of omission
Subsumption
Goodhart's law
The Coupling Effect

explanation.en: The lecture names Goodhart's law for this: once coverage is a target, shallow tests can raise the number. Faults of omission are a different limitation, namely missing code that coverage cannot detect.

prompt.en: What is the key idea of mutation testing?

en: It measures how much of the source code the tests execute
It repairs small faults in the code before testing begins
It tests the program by feeding random inputs to each function
It replaces real dependencies with mutants to isolate a unit
It tests the tests by injecting small faults they should detect

explanation.en: Mutation testing deliberately makes small changes (mutants) to the source code and checks whether the test suite detects them, so it tests the tests, not the program. Measuring how much code is executed is code coverage.

prompt.en: Who first proposed mutation testing, and when?

en: DeMillo, Lipton and Sayward, in 1978
Ammann and Offutt, in 2016
Richard Lipton, in 1971
Petrović and Ivanković, in 2018
Offutt et al., in 1996

explanation.en: Mutation testing was first proposed by Richard Lipton in 1971; DeMillo, Lipton and Sayward formalised it later, in 1978.

prompt.en: What is the name of the idea that tests which detect simple faults also tend to detect more complex faults made of several simple ones?

en: Goodhart's law
The Competent Programmer Hypothesis
The RIP model
Mutation score
The Coupling Effect

explanation.en: The Coupling Effect says tests that detect simple faults also tend to detect complex ones. The Competent Programmer Hypothesis instead says programmers write nearly correct code, so real faults are small deviations such as < instead of <=.

prompt.en: A mutant is run against the test suite and all tests pass. What is the correct conclusion and next step?

en: It survived; check whether it is equivalent or a test is missing
It survived; delete the tests that passed on the mutant
It is stillborn; discard it and leave it out of the count
It was killed; merge the mutant into the original program
It was killed; the tests detected the change, so move on

explanation.en: If all tests pass, the mutant survived; a mutant is killed only when at least one test fails. The survivor is analysed (equivalent or missing test?), and new or improved tests, which must pass on the original, are added.

prompt.en: A generated mutant does not compile. What is it called, and how is it handled?

en: A stillborn mutant; it is counted as a killed mutant
A killed mutant; it raises the mutation score
A stillborn mutant; it is discarded and not counted
An equivalent mutant; it is subtracted after inspection
A survived mutant; it reveals a weakness in the tests

explanation.en: A mutant that does not compile is stillborn; it is discarded before counting and does not enter the mutation score. Equivalent mutants do compile but behave exactly like the original.

prompt.en: A tool generates 120 mutants, and 20 of them do not compile. The tests kill 72 of the remaining mutants and 28 survive. Inspection shows that 10 of the survivors are equivalent. What is the mutation score according to the lecture's formula?

explanation.en: After discarding the 20 stillborn mutants, 100 remain, so the score is 72 / (100 − 10) × 100 = 80%. The value 72% (killed / total) is what many tools report, because equivalent mutants are usually unknown.

prompt.en: A test executes a mutated statement, and afterwards the program state differs from that of the original program. The test has no assertion on the affected output, so the mutant survives. Which RIP condition fails?

en: Equivalence
Infection
Reachability
Propagation
Coupling

explanation.en: Reachability (the mutated statement runs) and infection (the state differs) both hold, but propagation also requires the incorrect state to reach the output and an assertion in the test to check it.

prompt.en: Which conditions of the RIP model does code coverage guarantee?

en: Reachability, infection and propagation
Propagation only
Reachability only
Reachability and infection
Infection and propagation

explanation.en: Code coverage only guarantees that the code was executed (reachability). Killing a mutant requires reachability, infection and propagation, which is why coverage is not enough.

en: The mutant survives, because both versions give c = 3
The mutant is killed, because a + b exceeds 1007
The mutant is stillborn, because 1007 cannot be compiled
The mutant is killed, because the constant has changed
The mutant is equivalent, so no test could ever kill it

explanation.en: With such small inputs both versions compute c = 3, so the test passes and the mutant survives. It is not equivalent: larger inputs give different results, so the choice of test data matters.

prompt.en: A decision mutation changes if (a < b) to if (a <= b). Which test input can kill this mutant?

explanation.en: The two decisions differ only when a == b (a < b is false, a <= b is true), so only such a test can kill the mutant; this is why boundary-value tests matter. Changing < to > would be easy to kill, since almost any test with a ≠ b detects it.

prompt.en: A mutant is created by removing a method call from the code. Which type of mutation is this?

en: Decision mutation
Stillborn mutation
Equivalent mutation
Statement mutation
Value mutation

explanation.en: Statement mutations delete, duplicate or replace a statement, such as removing a method call. Value mutations change constant values, and decision mutations change operators in a decision, such as < to > or && to ||.

en: The loop body is never executed by any test in the suite
The test suite lacks an assertion that checks the value of sum
Coverage tools do not instrument the conditions of for loops
The mutant does not compile, so it is discarded before testing
Both loops run exactly ten times, so the behaviour is identical

explanation.en: This is an equivalent mutant: the code changed but the behaviour did not. Deciding equivalence is undecidable in general, so surviving mutants often have to be inspected manually, which is one of the main costs of mutation testing.

prompt.en: Which statement about mutation testing is correct?

en: It is a weaker criterion than statement coverage
Tools can detect all equivalent mutants automatically
It costs about one run of the test suite, like coverage
It can be applied without access to the source code
Detecting mutants is correlated with detecting real faults

explanation.en: Empirical studies show that detecting mutants is correlated with detecting real faults. Mutation testing is expensive (tests run for every mutant), needs the source code, requires manual inspection of equivalent mutants, and with suitable operators is stronger than statement and branch coverage.

sets.title: Week 5: Integration Testing and API Testing with Postman

prompt.en: A test sends POST /orders to a running service that writes to a real database. How is this test classified?

en: An integration test by interface and an API test by level
An API test, which is its own level between integration and system
A system test by level and a UI test by interface
An API test by interface and an integration test by level
A unit test by level and a code test by interface

explanation.en: Test level (how big the piece is) and test interface (where you touch the system) are independent questions: an HTTP request is the API interface, and a service with a real database is the integration level. API is an interface, not a level.

prompt.en: What caused the loss of the Mars Climate Orbiter in 1999?

en: Ground software sent pound-force seconds; navigation expected newton seconds
Expired credentials blocked ground software from reaching navigation
The navigation module failed its own unit tests but was launched anyway
Ground software called the navigation module in the wrong order
Navigation software received null values for the thruster impulse

explanation.en: Each module passed its own tests; the defect lived in the interface, where thruster impulse in pound-force seconds was read as newton seconds, off by a factor of 4.45.

prompt.en: A team tests how its online shop works together with an external payment provider that it does not own. Which kind of integration testing is this?

en: Component integration testing, because the two parts exchange data through an API
Acceptance testing, because the provider decides which payments are accepted
Unit testing, because the payment provider counts as one external module
Component integration testing, because both parts belong to the same system
System integration testing, because the provider is a system the team does not own

explanation.en: System integration testing covers your system and systems you do not own, such as a payment provider; component integration testing covers parts inside one system, such as the order service and its database.

prompt.en: A service starts returning null for a field that its caller assumes is always present, and the caller crashes. Which typical interface defect is this?

en: Call order
Error handling
Missing data
Configuration
Data mismatch

explanation.en: Missing data covers missing fields or unexpected null values; data mismatch would mean differing formats or units such as dates or currency.

prompt.en: Which statement correctly compares big-bang and incremental integration?

en: Big-bang makes defects easy to locate, but needs stubs or drivers
Big-bang needs no stubs or drivers, but a failure could come from anywhere
Big-bang reveals defects early, but needs more planning
Incremental needs no stubs or drivers, but testing starts late
Incremental combines all modules first, then tests the whole system

explanation.en: Big-bang combines everything at once, so it needs no stubs or drivers but failures are hard to locate and testing starts late. Incremental integration finds defects early and locates them easily, at the cost of stubs or drivers and more planning.

prompt.en: The UI calls the order and payment services, which call the database layer and the bank adapter. Only the database layer and the bank adapter are finished so far. Which approach fits?

en: Bottom-up integration, with stubs replacing the unfinished UI and services
Bottom-up integration, with drivers calling the database layer and bank adapter
Top-down integration, with drivers standing in for the unfinished UI
Top-down integration, with stubs replacing the database layer and bank adapter
Big-bang integration, with stubs replacing the unfinished services

explanation.en: Bottom-up starts with the low-level modules, and drivers act as the callers that are not ready yet. Stubs replace called modules, which is what top-down needs below the UI.

prompt.en: Which drawback belongs to bottom-up integration rather than top-down integration?

en: Testing cannot start until every module is combined
Low-level defects show up late in the integration
A failure could come from anywhere in the system
Nothing is visible until late in the integration
Modules below the UI must be replaced by stubs

explanation.en: Bottom-up tests low-level logic early but nothing is visible until late; top-down gives an early working skeleton, but its low-level defects show up late.

prompt.en: What is a driver in integration testing?

en: A fake callee that stands in for a called module and returns canned answers
A simplified but working implementation, such as an in-memory database
A fake caller that calls the module under test because the real caller is not ready
A server that simulates a third-party API and returns errors or delays on demand
A stub that also checks which operation was called, how often and with what data

explanation.en: A driver is a fake caller of the module under test; the fake callee on the other side that returns fixed, canned answers is a stub.

prompt.en: A test replaces the email service with a test double that returns "sent" and also checks that it was called exactly once with the customer's address. What kind of test double is this?

en: A stub
A container
A driver
A fake
A mock

explanation.en: A mock is a stub that also checks how it was called: which operation, how often and with what data. A plain stub only returns fixed, canned answers.

prompt.en: Which statement about the test pyramid is true?

en: Integration and API tests find interface defects unit tests miss, but can fail for more reasons
Integration and API tests are the fastest and cheapest, so they form the base
The pyramid is a strict law, so teams should never deviate from its proportions
Unit tests sit at the top because they are the slowest but most realistic tests
End-to-end UI tests should be the most numerous because they are closest to real use

explanation.en: The pyramid (a heuristic, not a law) has many fast, cheap unit tests at the bottom, some integration/API tests that catch interface defects but can fail due to network, data or timing, and few slow end-to-end tests at the top.

prompt.en: For an integration test's dependencies, which option gives the highest realism but the lowest speed?

en: A mock server that simulates a third-party API you do not control
A fake, such as an in-memory database used instead of the real one
A real database started in a container for each run, e.g. with Testcontainers
A driver that calls the module under test in place of the real caller
A stub that returns fixed, canned answers for every call

explanation.en: A real dependency in a container has high realism but low speed; a fake has medium realism and high speed, and a mock server has low realism and high speed.

prompt.en: You want to test how your system behaves when a third-party payment API you do not control answers with an error or a long delay. Which setup fits best?

en: A driver that calls the real payment API directly
A big-bang run against the provider's live service
A real payment API started in a container for each run
An in-memory fake that replaces the order database
A mock server that returns errors or delays on demand

explanation.en: A mock server simulates a third-party API you do not control and can return errors or delays on demand; containers are for real dependencies such as a database or message broker.

prompt.en: How is an HTTP request structured?

en: First line: method and path; then headers; after a blank line: the body
First line: status code; then headers; after a blank line: the body
First line: the body; then headers; after a blank line: method and path
First line: method and path; then the body; after a blank line: headers
First line: headers; then method and path; after a blank line: the body

explanation.en: The first line holds the method and path (e.g. POST /orders), the next lines are headers (metadata), and the body, often JSON, follows the blank line. A status code belongs to the response, not the request.

prompt.en: What is the difference between the HTTP methods PUT and PATCH?

en: PUT creates a new resource; PATCH removes it
PUT replaces a resource; PATCH partly updates it
PUT partly updates a resource; PATCH replaces it
PUT reads a resource; PATCH creates a new one
PUT removes a resource; PATCH reads it back

explanation.en: PUT replaces and PATCH partly updates a resource; creating is POST, reading is GET and removing is DELETE.

prompt.en: Which of these status codes signals a server error?

en: 400 Bad Request
404 Not Found
401 Unauthorized
503 Service Unavailable
204 No Content

explanation.en: The first digit gives the family: 5xx codes such as 500 and 503 are server errors, 4xx codes are client errors and 2xx codes are success.

prompt.en: An API answers POST /orders with 201 Created and a correct body, but the order is never stored. Which of the six API-test checks catches this defect?

en: Side effects: read the order back, e.g. with GET /orders/42
Response time: check that it is within the agreed limit
Headers: check Content-Type, Location and security headers
Status code: compare it with the code the specification promises
Schema: check that every required field has the right type

explanation.en: Only the side-effect check verifies that the action really happened, by reading the order back; the status code, body, schema, headers and response time can all look correct while nothing was saved.

prompt.en: In an API test, what is the difference between checking the schema and checking body values?

en: Schema checks the response time; body values check the side effects
Schema checks the response headers; body values check the status code
Schema checks the request that was sent; body values check the response
Schema checks the data is correct; body values check required fields and their types
Schema checks required fields and their types; body values check the data is correct

explanation.en: A schema check confirms that every required field is present with the right type, while a body-value check confirms the returned data is correct, e.g. status is "received" and quantity is 2.

prompt.en: For POST /orders, quantity must be between 1 and 10. Which responses do the boundary tests quantity = 0, 1, 10, 11 expect, in that order?

explanation.en: 0 and 11 lie just outside the valid range and are rejected with 400, while 1 and 10 are valid boundaries that create the order with 201; a 5xx would mean the API did not fail politely.

prompt.en: A negative test sends POST /orders without any token. Which status code should it expect?

en: 404 Not Found
500 Internal Server Error
401 Unauthorized
403 Forbidden
400 Bad Request

explanation.en: Sending no token gives 401; 403 (or 404) is expected when another customer's token is used to read someone else's order.

prompt.en: In Postman, what is an environment?

en: An ordered group of requests and their tests that is run as a whole
A CI workflow that runs the collection on every push and pull request
A report of one collection run written in JUnit format for CI
A set of variable values for one target, such as development, test or production
One HTTP call made up of a method, URL, headers and a body

explanation.en: An environment holds variable values for one target, like choosing which restaurant branch to visit; an ordered group of requests and tests is a collection, and a single HTTP call is a request.

prompt.en: What are scripts in Postman?

en: Ordered groups of requests that are run as a whole
Files that hold variable values for one target
JavaScript code that runs before or after a request
JUnit reports that are written after a collection run
Placeholders such as {{token}} reused across requests

explanation.en: Scripts are JavaScript run before (Pre-request) or after (Post-response) a request; placeholders such as {{token}} are variables, and per-target value sets are environments.

prompt.en: When does a Postman check written as pm.test(name, fn) pass?

en: When its function throws no error
When the response arrives within 500 ms
When its function returns true
When pm.response.json() returns a body
When the response status is 200

explanation.en: pm.test(name, fn) is one named check that passes if its function throws no error; a status code or response time is only checked when an assertion inside the function tests it.

prompt.en: Which line in a Post-response script asserts that the HTTP status code of the response is 201?

en: pm.test("status", 201);
pm.response.to.have.status(201);
pm.expect(pm.response.responseTime).to.eql(201);
pm.environment.set("status", 201);
pm.expect(pm.response.json().status).to.eql(201);

explanation.en: pm.response.to.have.status(201) checks the HTTP status code; pm.response.json().status reads the body field "status" (e.g. "received"), not the status code.

prompt.en: POST /auth returns {"token": "abc123"}. Which Post-response line saves the token so that later requests can send Authorization: Bearer {{token}}?

en: pm.environment.get("token", pm.response.json().token);
pm.test("token", pm.response.json().token);
pm.response.set("token", pm.environment.token);
pm.expect("token").to.eql(pm.response.json().token);
pm.environment.set("token", pm.response.json().token);

explanation.en: pm.environment.set stores the value as the variable token, which later requests reuse through {{token}}; pm.expect and pm.test only check values and store nothing.

prompt.en: Which Postman CLI command runs the collection orders.json once per row of a CSV file?

en: postman collection run orders.json -e orders.csv
postman collection run orders.csv -d orders.json
postman collection run orders.json --bail orders.csv
postman collection run orders.json -d orders.csv
postman collection run orders.json -r orders.csv

explanation.en: -d supplies the data file for a data-driven run with one iteration per CSV row; -e selects an environment and -r chooses reporters such as cli,junit.

prompt.en: By default, what happens when a test fails during a Postman CLI collection run?

en: The failure is reported and the run continues with the remaining requests
The failure is reported, but the run ends with exit code zero
The failing test is removed from the collection before the next run
The run stops at the first failure and skips the remaining requests
The failed request is retried until its test passes

explanation.en: By default every request runs and failed tests are reported; only --bail stops the run at the first failure, and any failed test still gives a non-zero exit code.

prompt.en: Which statement about Newman, compared with the Postman CLI, is true?

en: It is closed source and digitally signed by Postman
It also offers monitors, mocks and spec linting
It is open source and runs v2.1 JSON collections only
It is actively developed by Postman as of 2026
It runs both v2.1 JSON and v3 YAML collections

explanation.en: Newman is open source (since 2014), supports only v2.1 JSON and is no longer maintained (2026); closed source, v3 YAML support and monitors or mocks describe the Postman CLI.

prompt.en: In a CI pipeline that runs a Postman collection, what turns a failed API test into a red build?

en: The workflow is triggered by a pull request
The collection run ends with a non-zero exit code
The JUnit report is written to postman-cli-reports/
The Test Results tab shows a failed test
The --bail option stops the run early

explanation.en: Any failed test gives a non-zero exit code, and that exit code is how the CI server knows the build failed and stops the change before it reaches users.

prompt.en: A collection needs an API key when it runs in GitHub Actions. Where should the key be kept?

en: In the collection JSON, typed into every request header
In the CSV data file used for the data-driven run
In the environment file committed next to the collection
In the CI secret store, passed to the run as an environment variable
In the workflow YAML file under .github/workflows/

explanation.en: Secrets such as API keys and passwords live in the CI secret store and are passed as environment variables; they must never be committed to the repository.

prompt.en: In the chart of nine API test types, how does stress testing differ from load testing?

en: Stress simply checks whether the APIs are working; load tests against external threats
Stress sends unexpected data to find vulnerabilities; load compares results of old and new apps
Stress tests interactions between the UI and APIs; load tests several API calls together
Load deliberately creates high loads to see if APIs still work; stress tests capacity by simulating loads
Stress deliberately creates high loads to see if APIs still work; load tests capacity by simulating loads

explanation.en: The chart describes load testing as testing the application's capacity by simulating loads, and stress testing as deliberately creating high loads to see whether the APIs still function normally.

prompt.en: Which pairing of a test type and a suggested topic to look up is correct?

en: Performance testing: Pact
Security testing: OWASP API Security Top 10
Security testing: consumer-driven contracts
Contract testing: k6 or JMeter
Performance testing: OpenAPI

explanation.en: OWASP API Security Top 10 belongs to security testing; OpenAPI, consumer-driven contracts and Pact belong to contract testing, and k6 or JMeter to performance testing.

sets.title: Week 6: Advanced Test Design: Graph Coverage, Data Flow, Decision Tables

prompt.en: In a control flow graph (CFG), what does a node represent?

en: A possible transfer of control from one statement or block to the next
One combination of conditions together with the actions that follow from it
A statement, or a block of statements that always run one after another
A place where a variable gets a value, such as an assignment or input
A state the system stays in until a specific event moves it to another

explanation.en: A CFG node is a single statement or a block of statements that always execute in sequence; a possible transfer of control between nodes is an edge, not a node.

prompt.en: Which ISTQB coverage measure corresponds to Ammann and Offutt's edge coverage?

en: Prime path coverage
Decision table coverage
All-uses coverage
Statement coverage
Branch coverage

explanation.en: ISTQB calls edge coverage branch coverage and measures it as branches exercised divided by all branches; statement coverage is the ISTQB name for node coverage.

prompt.en:
The control flow graph of this function has one node per line plus a single exit node:
1 def classify(x, y):
2     if x > 0:
3         if y > 0:
4             return "both positive"
5         return "x positive, y non-positive"
6     return "x non-positive"
What node and edge coverage does the single test classify(-5, 3) reach?

en: Node coverage 57%, edge coverage 37.5%
Node coverage 50%, edge coverage 37.5%
Node coverage 67%, edge coverage 43%
Node coverage 37.5%, edge coverage 57%
Node coverage 57%, edge coverage 50%

explanation.en: The graph has 7 nodes (lines 1-6 and exit) and 8 edges; the path 1 → 2 → 6 → exit visits 4 of 7 nodes (57%) and takes 3 of 8 edges (37.5%), so the same test gives two different numbers.

prompt.en:
A test suite for this function already contains classify(-5, 3):
1 def classify(x, y):
2     if x > 0:
3         if y > 0:
4             return "both positive"
5         return "x positive, y non-positive"
6     return "x non-positive"
Which two added tests bring edge coverage to 100%?

en: classify(5, 0) and classify(3, -1)
classify(5, 3) and classify(5, -2)
classify(5, 3) and classify(-5, -3)
classify(-5, -3) and classify(5, -2)
classify(0, 3) and classify(5, 0)

explanation.en: classify(-5, 3) never reaches line 3, so the added tests must take both edges of the inner decision: classify(5, 3) goes from line 3 to line 4 and classify(5, -2) goes from line 3 to line 5. Every other pair misses the edge to line 4 or the edge to line 5 (x = 0 and y = 0 count as non-positive).

prompt.en: coverage.py with --branch is run after the single test classify(-5, 3). Line 2 of classify is if x > 0:, whose true branch goes to line 3 and whose false branch goes to line 6. The report shows line 2 in yellow as a partial branch. What does that mean?

en: Line 2 ran, and both of its branches were taken at least once
Line 2 ran, but the jump from line 2 to line 6 never happened
Line 2 never ran, so neither of its branches was taken
Line 2 ran, but the jump from line 2 to line 3 never happened
Line 2 defines a variable whose value is never used later

explanation.en: With x = -5, line 2 runs and jumps to line 6, but the jump 2 → 3 never happens, so the tool marks line 2 as a partial branch; lines that never ran are shown in red instead.

prompt.en: A graph has the edges A→B, A→C, B→D, C→D, D→E, D→F and E→F. The two tests A-B-D-E-F and A-C-D-F take every edge. Which of these edge pairs through the join node D is left uncovered?

en: B → D → E
A → C → D
A → B → D
B → D → F
C → D → F

explanation.en: D has 2 in-edges and 2 out-edges, so there are 2 × 2 = 4 pairs through it; the tests take only B → D → E and C → D → F, leaving B → D → F and C → D → E uncovered. Edge-pair coverage asks for all four, so it also tests how the first decision combines with the second.

prompt.en: Which description defines a prime path?

en: A path from a definition to a use with no other definition on it
A simple path that is not part of any longer simple path
A simple path that starts at the initial node of the graph
A path that starts at an initial node and ends at a final node
Any path of up to two edges that can be reached in the graph

explanation.en: A prime path is a simple path (no repeated node, except that it may start and end at the same node) that no longer simple path contains; a path from an initial to a final node is a test path.

prompt.en: A graph has the edges 1→2, 2→3, 3→4, 4→2 and 2→5, where node 5 is the exit. Which of these is a prime path?

explanation.en: [2, 3, 4, 2] is simple because only its first and last node are the same, and no longer simple path contains it. [1, 2, 3] and [2, 3, 4] sit inside [1, 2, 3, 4], [4, 2, 5] sits inside [3, 4, 2, 5], and [1, 2, 3, 4, 2] is not simple because node 2 repeats without being the start.

prompt.en: What does it mean that coverage criterion A subsumes criterion B?

en: A always needs fewer tests than B on the same graph
Every test set that satisfies B also satisfies A
A and B always need exactly the same set of tests
A measures control flow while B measures data flow
Every test set that satisfies A also satisfies B

explanation.en: Subsumption means that satisfying A guarantees B, as edge coverage guarantees node coverage; the reverse direction does not hold in general.

prompt.en: The code is if (x > 0) { y = 1; } with no else branch. What does the single test x = 1 achieve?

en: 100% node coverage but not 100% edge coverage
100% edge coverage but not 100% node coverage
100% node coverage and 100% edge coverage
100% edge-pair coverage but not 100% edge coverage
Neither 100% node coverage nor 100% edge coverage

explanation.en: With x = 1 every node is visited, but the false edge of the decision is never taken; this is why node coverage does not subsume edge coverage, while edge coverage does subsume node coverage.

prompt.en: In data flow testing, when is a path from a definition of a variable to a use of it def-clear?

en: When no other use of that variable lies on the path
When the variable is defined before the function is called
When the path visits every definition of that variable
When the path contains no decision nodes at all
When no other definition of that variable lies on the path

explanation.en: A def-clear path has no other definition of the variable between the def and the use; a def and a use joined by at least one such path form a du-pair.

prompt.en:
Which list gives every du-pair (def line, use line) for the variable price?
1  price = read_price()
2  if price > 100:
3      price = 100
4  print(price)

explanation.en: price is defined on lines 1 and 3 and used on lines 2 (p-use) and 4 (c-use); (1, 4) counts because 1 → 2 → 4 is def-clear, even though 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 is not. Line 3 only assigns price, so it is a def, not a use.

prompt.en:
In this bill code, which line holds a p-use of total?
1  total = 0
2  for item in order:
3      total = total + item.price
4  if total > 200:
5      total = total * 0.9
6  print(total)

en: Line 1, total = 0
Line 6, print(total)
Line 4, if total > 200:
Line 3, total = total + item.price
Line 5, total = total * 0.9

explanation.en: A p-use reads the variable inside a decision, as line 4 does; lines 3, 5 and 6 read total in a computation, which are c-uses, and line 1 is only a definition.

prompt.en:
Which test covers the du-pair (line 1, line 6) for total in this bill code?
1  total = 0
2  for item in order:
3      total = total + item.price
4  if total > 200:
5      total = total * 0.9
6  print(total)

en: An order whose items add up to exactly 200 TL
An order with two items of 120 TL each
An order with one item of 150 TL
An empty order, so the loop body never runs
