An order with one item of 250 TL

explanation.en: Any item runs line 3, which redefines total, so only an empty order gives the def-clear path 1 → 2 → 4 → 6 (with total = 0 the discount on line 5 is skipped as well).

prompt.en: Which statement correctly contrasts all-defs coverage with all-uses coverage?

en: All-defs: each def reaches at least one use; all-uses: each def reaches every use it can reach
All-defs: each def reaches at least one use; all-uses: every simple def-clear path is taken
All-defs: each def reaches every use it can reach; all-uses: each def reaches at least one use
All-defs: every def line is executed once; all-uses: every use line is executed once
All-defs: each variable is defined only once; all-uses: each variable is used only once

explanation.en: All-defs needs one def-clear path from every definition to at least one of its uses, while all-uses needs a def-clear path to every use the definition can reach; taking every simple def-clear path is the stronger all-du-paths criterion.

prompt.en: Which statement about all-du-paths coverage is true?

en: It never needs more tests than all-uses, even with loops in between
It is subsumed by all-defs, so all-defs tests always satisfy it
It needs every simple def-clear path from each def to each of its uses
It needs every path, including ones that repeat a loop many times
It needs only one def-clear path from each def to one of its uses

explanation.en: All-du-paths asks for every simple def-clear path from each definition to each of its uses and subsumes all-uses, which subsumes all-defs; it can need many more tests than all-uses when branches or loops lie between a def and its use.

prompt.en:
For the variable price in this code, which test set achieves all-uses coverage?
1  price = read_price()
2  if price > 100:
3      price = 100
4  print(price)

en: price = 50 only
price = 150 and price = 200
price = 50 and price = 80
price = 150 and price = 50
price = 150 only

explanation.en: price = 150 runs 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 and covers (1, 2) and (3, 4), which is already enough for all-defs; all-uses also needs (1, 4), which a value of 100 or less such as price = 50 covers through 1 → 2 → 4.

prompt.en:
In this function body, total is not assigned anywhere else:
for item in order:
    total = total + item.price
print(total)
Which data flow anomaly does it contain?

en: item is defined and never used
total is used before any definition
total is defined twice with no use in between
item is used before any definition
total is defined and never used

explanation.en: On the first iteration total + item.price reads total before anything has assigned it, so the program reads a default or leftover value where the language does not stop this at compile time. Every definition of total is followed by a use, and item is defined by the loop and used in item.price.

prompt.en: Which order lists the graph coverage criteria from strongest to weakest, as in the subsumption ladder?

en: Complete path, edge-pair, prime path, edge, node
Complete path, prime path, edge-pair, node, edge
Prime path, complete path, edge-pair, edge, node
Complete path, prime path, edge, edge-pair, node
Complete path, prime path, edge-pair, edge, node

explanation.en: In the ladder each criterion subsumes the one below it, from complete path down to edge coverage (ISTQB branch coverage) and finally node coverage (ISTQB statement coverage); the one dashed arrow holds only on graphs without self-loops.

prompt.en: A restaurant gives students 10% off and a free dessert with orders over 400 TL, but both offers end at 18:00. With the true/false conditions "student", "order over 400 TL" and "before 18:00", how many columns does the full decision table have before minimization?

en: 8 columns
6 columns
3 columns
9 columns
5 columns

explanation.en: A full decision table has a column for every combination, so n true/false conditions give 2^n columns: 2^3 = 8. Merging columns comes only afterwards, during minimization.

prompt.en: In the tutorial's login decision table, what does the Combinations column list for the rule whose expected result is "Enter valid credentials to login"?

en: Both valid; either of them valid
NA, because only one combination applies
Both blank; either of them blank
Both invalid; either of them invalid
User id blank; password invalid

explanation.en: That row lists "Both invalid" and "Either of them invalid"; "Both blank" and "Either of them blank" belong to the rule that asks for non-blank credentials, and the Login rule shows NA.

prompt.en: In ISTQB decision table notation, how do the condition entries "-" and "N/A" differ?

en: "-" means the combination is infeasible; N/A means the condition does not affect the outcome
"-" means the condition does not affect the outcome; N/A means the combination is infeasible
"-" means the action does not happen; N/A means the action happens for this rule
They mean the same thing; N/A is only an older way of writing the dash "-"
"-" means the condition is not satisfied; N/A means the column has not been tested yet

explanation.en: ISTQB writes "-" for a condition that does not matter and keeps N/A for combinations that cannot happen. The tutorial's NA means "does not matter", so it corresponds to the ISTQB dash.

prompt.en: The full login decision table has four columns for C1 (both fields filled?) and C2 (valid user id and password?). Why does the minimized table have only three columns?

en: When C1 is F the outcome is the same for either value of C2, so two columns merge
Columns that lead to any error message are combined into one single column
When C2 is T the outcome is the same for either value of C1, so two columns merge
The "Log in" action needs no separate test, so its column is removed
The combination of a blank field with valid credentials is infeasible, so it is dropped

explanation.en: With a blank field the system asks for non-blank credentials whatever C2 is, so columns 1 and 2 merge into R1 with C2 = "-"; the combination is not infeasible, its C2 value simply does not matter.

prompt.en: According to the tutorial's rules for turning a logical flow diagram into a decision table, what must the finished table do?

en: Hold one boundary value from every partition in each of its rules
List the decision boxes as results and the leaves as validations
Include only the leaves that end in a successful result
Leave out results that can be reached by more than one combination
Cover every branch and every leaf (result) of the logical tree

explanation.en: The validations in the decision boxes become columns of the table and every result (leaf) of the flow diagram must be covered; after completing the table one verifies that all branches and leaves of the logical tree are covered.

prompt.en: A decision table has 8 columns, 2 of which are infeasible combinations. The tests exercise 3 of the feasible columns. What is the decision table coverage?

explanation.en: The coverage items are only the feasible columns, so coverage is 3 / 6 = 50%; dividing by all 8 columns (37.5%) wrongly counts the infeasible ones.

prompt.en: A login page passes the three tests that give 100% decision table coverage. Which aspect do these tests leave to equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis?

en: The feasible rules of the table, each exercised at least once
The rule that valid credentials lead to a successful login
The rule that a blank field triggers the non-blank alert
The rule that invalid credentials trigger the valid-credentials alert
The values inside a condition, such as how long a user id may be

explanation.en: 100% decision table coverage tests every rule once but not the values inside a condition, such as which field is blank, which password is wrong or how long a user id may be; equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis cover that part.

prompt.en: Which of these is an advantage of the decision table technique?

en: The table stays small no matter how many conditions there are
Missing or contradictory rules show up as empty or conflicting columns
A wrong rule in the table is caught by running the table's own tests
It tests behaviour that depends on the order of events over time
Boundary values and partitions fit directly into the table template

explanation.en: Gaps and contradictions in the rules appear as empty or conflicting columns. The table itself still needs a review, because a wrong rule in the table simply produces a wrong test.

prompt.en: An order can be placed, paid and then cancelled, and the correct result depends on the order in which these events happen. Which technique fits this behaviour better than a decision table?

en: Equivalence partitioning
Checklist-based testing
Boundary value analysis
State transition testing
Error guessing

explanation.en: A decision table describes combinations of conditions at one moment; when the result depends on the order of events, state transition testing fits better.

prompt.en: A password must be 8 to 16 characters long, which gives the length partitions 0-7, 8-16 and 17 and up. Which lengths does 3-value boundary value analysis select?

explanation.en: The boundaries are the smallest and largest value of every partition (0, 7, 8, 16, 17), and 3-value BVA adds both neighbours of each, while 0 has no lower neighbour. 0, 7, 8, 16, 17 alone is the 2-value set, and 4, 12, 20 is one equivalence partitioning value per partition.

prompt.en: In an order state machine with the states Placed, Paid, Shipped and Cancelled, cancelling a shipped order is rejected as an invalid transition. Which coverage level requires a test that attempts it?

en: All transitions, including attempts at invalid ones
All edges of the code's control flow graph
All feasible decision table columns
All states
All valid transitions

explanation.en: State transition coverage can target all states, all valid transitions, or all transitions including attempts at invalid ones; only the last level asks for a test such as cancelling a shipped order.

prompt.en: Which technique designs, runs and evaluates tests at the same time, often inside a fixed time box and with a short written charter?

en: Error guessing
Checklist-based testing
Decision table testing
State transition testing
Exploratory testing

explanation.en: This describes exploratory testing; error guessing relies on the tester's experience and lists of faults seen before, and checklist-based testing works through a prepared list of conditions.

prompt.en: A payment field offers the choices Cash, Card and Voucher, which have no order. Which statement is true?

en: Only 3-value boundary value analysis applies to such a list
Both apply, with Cash and Voucher used as the boundary values
Neither applies, because the input is not a number
Equivalence partitioning applies, but boundary value analysis does not
Boundary value analysis applies, but equivalence partitioning does not

explanation.en: Equivalence partitioning fits any kind of input, including options, while boundary value analysis needs values that have an order, so an unordered list of choices has no boundaries to test.

prompt.en: In the recommended steps for writing test cases for business logic, which step comes last, as a final touch?

en: Error guessing based on experience
Combinations and permutations for field-level validations
A decision table for every feasible rule combination
Boundary value analysis and equivalence partitioning
State transition testing of the business flow

explanation.en: The steps are a decision table first, then boundary value analysis and equivalence partitioning for input ranges, then combinations for field-level validations, and finally error guessing with experience as a final touch.

prompt.en: Which statement describes property-based testing, as opposed to traditional example-based testing?

en: Properties are stated and many test cases are generated automatically
Each test pairs one specific input with one expected output
Each property is checked against a single fixed input value
Test cases are hand-picked by the tester, which can add human bias
Every generated input needs a hand-written expected output

explanation.en: In property-based testing you specify properties that must always hold and the tool generates many random test cases (Test Case 1…N) to check them. One specific input with one expected output, chosen manually and prone to human bias, describes example-based testing.

prompt.en: In model-based testing, what is a model?

en: The smallest failing input found after shrinking
A simplified, abstract representation of the real system
A boolean condition that must hold for every valid input
A highly optimised version of the production implementation
A component that produces random input data for tests

explanation.en: A model is a simplified, abstract representation that is easier to reason about than the real implementation. A boolean condition that always holds is a property, and producing random data is the job of a generator.

prompt.en: A team applies model-based testing to a highly optimised Set implementation. Which model matches the course example?

en: A second, equally optimised Set written by another team
A random generator that produces integer lists
A simple List that keeps every duplicate it is given
A simple List plus the rule that no duplicates are allowed
A sorting function whose output is always ordered

explanation.en: The complex implementation is compared against a simple, trusted model: a List with the rule "no duplicates allowed". Another optimised Set is not simpler, and a List that keeps duplicates would not behave like a Set.

prompt.en: Which pair of properties is given for a sorting function?

en: The output is sorted and reversing it twice yields the input
The output equals the input and contains no duplicate elements
The output is sorted and contains exactly the same elements as the input
The output is the reversed input and has the same length
The output is sorted and is always shorter than the input

explanation.en: For a sorting function the listed properties are that the output is sorted and contains exactly the same elements as the input. Reversing twice gives back the list that was reversed (the output), not the original input.

prompt.en: In model-based testing, the same random sequence of operations has been run on both the model and the real system. What is the next step?

en: Discard the model and keep only the real system's output
Replace the real system with the model in production
Define the same operations for the model and the real system
Define an abstract model of the system under test
Compare the states and outputs of the model and the real system

explanation.en: The steps are: define an abstract model, define the same operations for model and real system, generate random operation sequences, run them on both, then compare states and outputs. Defining the model and operations happens earlier.

prompt.en: In the guidance on when to use each approach, which kind of target is listed for model-based testing rather than plain property-based testing?

en: String manipulation and parsing routines
Specific use cases checked with one fixed example
Pure functions that have no side effects
State machines such as protocols or device states
Mathematical functions and algorithms

explanation.en: State machines (protocols, device states), APIs and complex workflows are listed under model-based testing. Pure functions, string manipulation/parsing and mathematical functions/algorithms are listed under property-based testing, and specific use cases suit example-based testing.

prompt.en: In property-based testing, what is the role of a generator?

en: Reporting how many generated tests have passed
Stating a boolean condition that must hold
Producing random input data for the property
Minimizing a failing test case to a simpler one
Comparing system outputs against a trusted model

explanation.en: The core ingredients are generators (produce random input data), properties (boolean true/false conditions) and shrinking (minimize failing test cases).

prompt.en: In QuickCheck (Haskell), what provides random data generation?

en: The @Provide annotation
The @Property annotation
The JUnit Jupiter engine
The @ForAll annotation
The Arbitrary typeclass

explanation.en: QuickCheck uses the Arbitrary typeclass for random data generation. @ForAll, @Provide and @Property are jqwik annotations, and JUnit 5 (Jupiter) is the framework jqwik integrates with.

prompt.en:
Given this Haskell code:
prop_reverse :: [Int] -> Bool
prop_reverse xs = reverse (reverse xs) == xs
main = quickCheck prop_reverse
What does quickCheck prop_reverse do by default?

en: Generates 100 random integer lists and runs the property on each
Checks every possible integer list exhaustively before reporting
Runs the property once on a fixed list chosen by the tester
Compares the reverse function against a simple model of a list
Generates random lists until the property passes once, then stops

explanation.en: quickCheck uses the Arbitrary instance for [Int] to generate many random lists (100 by default) and runs prop_reverse on each, printing "+++ OK, passed 100 tests." or reporting a counter-example if one fails.

prompt.en: Which of these has the form of a composition property?

en: reverse (reverse xs) == xs
f (g x) == h x
f(x) == x
insert preserves membership
sort result is ordered

explanation.en: Composition is written f (g x) == h x. f(x) == x is identity, reverse (reverse xs) == xs is involution, and the sort/insert statements are collection properties.

en: A separate @Provide method is required to build each list
The tester supplies one fixed list inside the method body
They are shrunk counter-examples saved from a prior run
jqwik automatically generates many List<Integer> values
JUnit 5 reads the lists from an external CSV data file

explanation.en: @ForAll asks jqwik to supply random values for that parameter, so jqwik automatically generates many List<Integer> values and checks the property for all of them. @Provide is only needed for named custom generators.

prompt.en: In jqwik, how is a named custom generator defined and used?

en: Defined with @Property and used via @ForAll("name")
Defined with @Provide and used via @ForAll("name")
Defined with @Provide and used via @Property("name")
Defined with @ForAll and used via @Provide("name")
Defined as an Arbitrary typeclass and used via quickCheck

explanation.en: Named generators are declared with @Provide and referenced with @ForAll("name"). @Property marks the property method itself, and the Arbitrary typeclass with quickCheck belongs to Haskell's QuickCheck.

prompt.en:
A jqwik generator is defined as:
Arbitraries.strings()
    .withCharRange('a', 'z')
    .ofMinLength(1).ofMaxLength(5)
Which value could it generate?

en: "ABC"
"abcde"
"abcdef"
"ab1"

explanation.en: The generator yields strings of length 1–5 made of lowercase letters a–z. The empty string is too short, "abcdef" is too long, and uppercase letters or digits are outside the character range.

prompt.en: When a property fails, what is the goal of shrinking?

en: Finding the smallest, simplest failing example
Simplifying the property until it passes again
Reducing the number of generated test runs
Removing the failing input from the test report
Compressing generated data to save memory

explanation.en: jqwik/QuickCheck shrink the failing input to the smallest, simplest failing example (e.g. a 100-element list down to maybe 2 elements), which makes debugging much easier.

prompt.en: A jqwik property encodes the intuition that in Java a % b is always between 0 and b - 1. Which input is a counter-example?

en: a = 3, b = 2 (result 1)
a = 5, b = 3 (result 2)
a = 4, b = 2 (result 0)
a = 1, b = 2 (result 1)
a = -1, b = 2 (result -1)

explanation.en: In Java, modulo with a negative a can be negative, so -1 % 2 == -1 falls outside 0 to b - 1, a language-specific corner case. The other inputs all give results inside that range.

prompt.en: Which of these is listed as a disadvantage of property-based testing?

en: All inputs must be chosen by hand
Boundary cases are often missed
Good properties are harder to define
Only a limited number of inputs is used
Fewer chances to hit corner cases

explanation.en: The listed cons of property-based testing are that good properties are harder to define and it requires more abstract thinking. A limited number of inputs and missed boundary cases are the cons of example-based testing.

prompt.en: Which statement correctly compares QuickCheck and jqwik?

en: QuickCheck is the origin of property-based testing; jqwik fits into JUnit 5
jqwik is mainly backed by the functional programming community
jqwik is the origin of property-based testing; QuickCheck fits into JUnit 5
Only jqwik shrinks failing inputs; QuickCheck only reports the first failure
Only QuickCheck generates random data; jqwik relies on fixed examples

explanation.en: QuickCheck (Haskell) is the origin of property-based testing with strong functional-programming support, while jqwik fits naturally into JUnit 5 test suites. Both provide random generation and shrinking.

prompt.en: Which statement about property-based testing in industry is correct?

en: It weakens regression suites by replacing fixed examples
Teams used to example-based thinking may resist it at first
It has no learning curve for developers or testers
It is rarely used in finance, telecom or network protocols
It increases the effort of manual test case design

explanation.en: Challenges include a learning curve and initial resistance from teams used to example-based thinking. Its advantages are stronger regression suites and less manual test case design, and it is used in finance, telecom and network protocols.

sets.title: Week 8: Performance and Reliability in Test Engineering

prompt.en: In the 'dual mandate' of modern engineering, how do the performance and reliability pillars differ in focus?

en: Performance focuses on repairable systems; reliability on non-repairable ones
Performance focuses on endurance over time; reliability on behavior now
Performance focuses on data volume; reliability on concurrent users
Performance focuses on failure rates; reliability on response times
Performance focuses on behavior now; reliability on endurance over time

explanation.en: Performance excellence means being fast, responsive and efficient under load to meet immediate demands (behavior now). Reliability assurance means operating without failure over the entire lifecycle (endurance over time).

prompt.en: In terms of which aspects does performance testing evaluate a system?

en: Responsiveness, stability and resource usage under workload
Infant mortality, useful life and wear-out behaviour
Failure rate, MTTF and MTBF over the system's lifecycle
Statement, branch and path coverage of the code
Survival probability beyond a specified time t

explanation.en: Performance testing evaluates responsiveness, stability and resource usage under workload, asking for example how fast the system responds and how many concurrent users it can handle. Failure rates, MTTF/MTBF and bathtub phases belong to reliability.

prompt.en: Which type of performance test applies a sustained load over an extended period?

en: Stress testing
Scalability testing
Spike testing
Endurance (soak) testing
Volume testing

explanation.en: Endurance (soak) testing applies a sustained load for an extended period. Spike testing uses sudden dramatic increases in load, stress testing goes beyond normal capacity, and volume testing uses large amounts of data.

prompt.en: When ticket sales open, a website's traffic suddenly jumps to many times its usual level within seconds. Which performance test simulates this situation?

en: Scalability testing
Load testing
Spike testing
Volume testing
Endurance (soak) testing

explanation.en: Spike testing simulates sudden dramatic increases in load. Load testing simulates the expected user load, and endurance testing holds a load for an extended period.

prompt.en: How does stress testing differ from load testing?

en: Stress simulates expected load; load pushes beyond normal capacity
Stress pushes beyond normal capacity; load simulates expected load
Stress checks scaling up or out; load checks recovery from failure
Stress holds the load for days; load uses sudden bursts of traffic
Stress uses large amounts of data; load uses many concurrent users

explanation.en: Load testing simulates the expected user load, while stress testing pushes the system beyond its normal capacity. Large amounts of data are volume testing, and a long sustained load is endurance (soak) testing.

prompt.en: In performance testing, what does throughput measure?

en: Transactions per unit time, such as TPS or RPS
The time between a request and its response
The probability of failure by time t
CPU, memory and disk I/O consumption
The percentage of requests that fail

explanation.en: Throughput is transactions per unit time (TPS/RPS). The time between request and response is response time, the percentage of failed requests is the error rate, and CPU/memory/disk I/O is resource utilization.

prompt.en: Which target values does the lecture give for CPU utilization and for the error rate in production?

en: CPU below 90%, error rate below 0.1%
CPU below 50%, error rate below 5%
CPU below 80%, error rate below 5%
CPU below 80%, error rate below 1%
CPU below 95%, error rate below 1%

explanation.en: The lecture gives a CPU utilization target of less than 80% and an error-rate target of less than 1% for production.

prompt.en: What does the reliability function R(t) = P(T > t) give, where T is the time to failure?

en: The probability that the system is operational at any given time
The average time between two consecutive failures
The probability that the system survives beyond time t
The probability that the system has failed by time t
The instantaneous rate of failure at time t

explanation.en: R(t) is the probability of survival beyond time t. The probability of failure by time t is the unreliability F(t) = 1 − R(t), and the probability of being operational at any given time is availability.

prompt.en: Which formula defines the failure rate (hazard function) λ(t)?

en: λ(t) = f(t) × R(t)
λ(t) = f(t) / R(t)
λ(t) = F(t) / R(t)
λ(t) = R(t) / f(t)

explanation.en: λ(t) = f(t) / R(t) is the instantaneous rate of failure at time t, given survival up to t. The expression 1 − R(t) is the unreliability F(t), not the failure rate.

prompt.en: In which phase of the bathtub curve is the failure rate constant, and what causes the failures in that phase?

en: Infant mortality; manufacturing defects and design flaws
Wear-out; age-related deterioration
Useful life; manufacturing defects and design flaws
Wear-out; random external events
Useful life; random external events

explanation.en: In the useful-life phase the failure rate is constant, failures come from random external events, and the phase is modeled by the exponential distribution. Manufacturing defects and design flaws cause infant mortality, and age-related deterioration causes wear-out.

prompt.en: A Weibull analysis of field data gives a shape parameter β = 0.6. Which phase of the bathtub curve does this indicate?

en: Wear-out, with a decreasing failure rate
Useful life, with a constant failure rate
Useful life, with an increasing failure rate
Infant mortality, with a decreasing failure rate
Wear-out, with an increasing failure rate

explanation.en: For the Weibull distribution, β < 1 indicates infant mortality (decreasing failure rate), β = 1 indicates useful life and β > 1 indicates wear-out.

prompt.en: What does the memoryless property of the exponential distribution mean?

en: A component's future reliability is independent of its current age
Failures cluster around an average lifetime of the component
A component's failure rate rises steadily as it gets older
The shape parameter β decides which failure phase applies
Early failures are weeded out, so the failure rate decreases

explanation.en: Memoryless means a component's future reliability is independent of its current age, which fits the constant failure rate of the useful-life phase. Failures clustering around an average lifetime describe the normal distribution.

prompt.en: Which statement about failure distributions is correct?

en: A Weibull distribution with β = 1 models wear-out failures
The exponential distribution has an increasing failure rate
The Weibull distribution can model all three bathtub phases
The normal distribution models infant mortality failures
The exponential distribution models the wear-out phase

explanation.en: The Weibull distribution is the 'Swiss Army Knife' of reliability: its shape parameter β lets it model infant mortality, useful life and wear-out. The exponential distribution models useful life (constant failure rate), and the normal distribution models wear-out.

prompt.en: Which statement about MTTF and MTBF is correct?

en: MTTF is the average time between consecutive failures
MTBF = MTTF + MTTR, and MTBF is used for repairable systems
MTBF is the expected time until the first failure
MTBF = MTTF − MTTR, and MTBF is used for non-repairable systems
MTTF = MTBF + MTTR, and MTTF is used for repairable systems

explanation.en: MTBF, the average time between consecutive failures, applies to repairable systems such as servers and equals MTTF + MTTR. MTTF is the expected time until the first failure and applies to non-repairable systems such as light bulbs.

prompt.en: A repairable system has MTBF = 495 hours and MTTR = 5 hours. What is its availability according to the lecture's formula?

explanation.en: Availability A = MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR) = 495 / (495 + 5) = 495 / 500 = 0.99, i.e. 99%.

prompt.en: How much annual downtime corresponds to 'four nines' (99.99%) availability?

en: 8.76 hours
87.6 minutes
52.6 hours
5.26 minutes
52.6 minutes

explanation.en: 99.99% ('four nines') allows 52.6 minutes of downtime per year, while 99.9% ('three nines') allows 8.76 hours and 99.999% ('five nines') allows 5.26 minutes.

prompt.en: Three components with reliabilities 0.9, 0.9 and 0.8 are connected in series. What is the system reliability?

explanation.en: In a series system R_system = R1 × R2 × R3 = 0.9 × 0.9 × 0.8 = 0.648. It is lower than the least reliable component (0.8), because the system fails if any single component fails.

prompt.en: Two identical components, each with reliability 0.9, are connected in parallel. What is the system reliability?

explanation.en: For a parallel system R_system = 1 − (1 − R)^n = 1 − (0.1)^2 = 0.99, higher than a single component because the system works if at least one component works. The value 0.81 would be the series result.

prompt.en: What does the lecture mean by performability?

en: A unified performance-reliability measure that allows degraded states
A test that pushes a system beyond its normal operating capacity
The number of transactions a system completes per unit of time
The probability that a system survives beyond a specified time t
The share of time a system is operational, MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR)

explanation.en: Performability is a unified measure combining performance and reliability, acknowledging that systems can operate in degraded states. Survival beyond time t is R(t), and MTBF / (MTBF + MTTR) is availability.

prompt.en: According to the causal chain linking performance to failure, why is performance monitoring also a form of reliability monitoring?

en: Performance metrics change only after the system has already failed
Rising response times or CPU use are early warnings of reliability issues
High load moves worn components back into the useful-life phase
High CPU utilization lowers λ(t) by weeding out weak components early
Response time and MTTF are calculated with the same formula

explanation.en: High performance demand increases system stress (CPU, memory, thermal load), which accelerates wear-out mechanisms and increases λ(t). Rising response times or CPU utilization are therefore early warnings that enable predictive maintenance.

prompt.en: In the performance-reliability trade-off matrix, where does an overclocked CPU running at its thermal limit with no resource buffers belong?

en: Living on the Edge: high performance, low reliability
Over-Engineered: low performance, high reliability
Well-Architected: high performance, high reliability
Unacceptable: low performance, low reliability
Living on the Edge: low performance, high reliability

explanation.en: An overclocked CPU at its thermal limit gives high performance but low reliability ('Living on the Edge'). A heavily derated component is Over-Engineered, and a load-balanced, fault-tolerant system with performance margins is the Well-Architected goal.

prompt.en: In the data center case study (10,000 servers, 99.99% availability required), how was automated failover tested?

en: Each server's MTBF was raised to 200,000 hours before testing
Weibull analysis modeled the degradation of server capacitors
A 5,000-hour thermal cycling test accelerated server aging
Load balancing was switched off to test each server alone
Performance tests were run during simulated server failures

explanation.en: The team ran performance testing during simulated server failure scenarios to test automated failover, on an N+1 redundant, load-balanced architecture; it achieved 99.995% availability. Thermal cycling and Weibull analysis of capacitors belong to the automotive ECU case study.

prompt.en: In the automotive ECU case study, what was Weibull analysis used for?

en: Checking that the real-time cycle time stayed below 10 ms
Modeling capacitor degradation, the primary wear-out failure mode
Converting the availability target into annual downtime
Simulating server failures to test automated failover
Modeling infant mortality caused by software design flaws

explanation.en: Weibull analysis modeled capacitor degradation, the primary wear-out failure mode; performance was tested separately at temperature extremes and in a 5,000-hour combined test with thermal cycling. The projected MTTF exceeded 200,000 hours.

prompt.en: A system has 10 parameters and each parameter has 5 possible values. How many test cases does testing every combination require?

explanation.en: Each of the 10 parameters independently takes one of 5 values, so there are 5^10 = 9,765,625 combinations; 10^5 swaps base and exponent. This is why testing all combinations is practically impossible.

prompt.en: A web application must be tested on 4 browsers, 3 operating systems, 3 screen resolutions, 3 languages and 2 themes. How many test cases does full exhaustive coverage require?

explanation.en: Exhaustive coverage multiplies the number of values per parameter: 4 × 3 × 3 × 3 × 2 = 216. Adding them (15) only counts the distinct values, not the combinations.

prompt.en: According to the Kuhn & Reilly (NIST, 2002) research cited in the lecture, roughly what share of software faults is caused by the interaction of two parameter values?

en: About 90%
About 30%
About 70%
About 50%
About 98%

explanation.en: The "90% rule" states that about 90% of faults are caused by the interaction of two parameter values. About 70% is the share caused by a single parameter value, and about 98% involves three or fewer parameters.

prompt.en: Which statement about where bugs hide matches the research presented in the lecture?

en: Most faults need interactions of four or more parameters to appear
About 98% of faults are caused by interactions of three or fewer parameters
About 90% of faults are caused by a single parameter value
Most critical bugs come from complex interactions of many parameters
About 70% of faults are caused by the interaction of two parameter values

explanation.en: The research reports about 70% single-parameter faults, about 90% two-parameter interactions and about 98% for three or fewer parameters. The most critical bugs are therefore found in simple interactions, not complex ones.

prompt.en: What does pairwise (2-way) testing guarantee about the generated test suite?

en: Every parameter is tested alone while the others keep default values
Every combination of all parameter values is tested exactly once
Each pair of parameters is tested with just one value combination
Every possible trio of values across all parameters is tested at least once
Every possible pair of values across all parameters is tested at least once

explanation.en: Instead of testing all combinations, pairwise testing covers every possible pair of values across all parameters at least once, so one value combination per parameter pair is not enough. Covering every trio is 3-way testing, and covering every full combination is exhaustive testing.

prompt.en: Parameters A, B and C each have two values (a1/a2, b1/b2, c1/c2). Which set of four tests achieves full pairwise coverage?

explanation.en: The set (a1,b1,c1), (a1,b2,c2), (a2,b1,c2), (a2,b2,c1) contains all four A-B, A-C and B-C value pairs, so 4 tests replace the 8 exhaustive combinations. Every other set misses at least one pair; for example, the set in which B and C always match never pairs b1 with c2.

prompt.en: Which test strength is described as a basic "smoke test" in which every value is tested once?

en: 3-way
Exhaustive testing
t-way with t = 4
2-way (pairwise)
1-way

explanation.en: 1-way testing only requires every value to be tested once, which the lecture calls a basic smoke test. 2-way testing covers every pair and is described as the industry workhorse.

prompt.en: Which statement about test strengths in t-way testing is correct?

en: 3-way testing covers every trio of values and is meant for high-risk systems
3-way testing tests each value only once and serves as a smoke test
1-way testing covers every pair of values and is the industry workhorse
2-way testing covers every trio of values and is meant for high-risk systems
t-way testing is a special case of pairwise testing where t is always 2

explanation.en: 3-way testing covers every trio of values and is suggested for high-risk systems, finding about 98% of faults. Pairwise testing is the special case t = 2 of the general t-way form, not the other way round.

prompt.en: What is the engineering trade-off when the strength t of combinatorial testing is increased?

en: The number of test cases drops because invalid combinations are removed
Fault detection rate increases, but so does the number of test cases
Both the fault detection rate and the number of test cases decrease
Fault detection rate increases while the number of test cases stays the same
Fault detection rate drops because each test becomes more complex

explanation.en: As t increases, the fault detection rate rises together with the number of test cases, moving from lower cost/fewer tests towards higher coverage/more tests. Removing invalid combinations is the job of constraints, not of raising t.

prompt.en: Which description fits PICT rather than ACTS?

en: NIST-backed tool known for its strong IPOG algorithm support
Tool nicknamed "The Researcher's Choice" for learning and analysis
Command-line driven Microsoft tool, ideal for CI/CD pipeline integration
Tool whose main strengths are its GUI and its NIST research backing
GUI-based NIST tool, excellent for learning and analysis

explanation.en: PICT (Pairwise Independent Combinatorial Testing) is Microsoft's open-source, command-line tool with a rich constraint language, called "The Automation Engineer's Ally". A GUI, IPOG algorithm support and NIST backing describe ACTS, "The Researcher's Choice".

prompt.en: Which sequence correctly describes generating tests with PICT?

en: List only seeded test cases, run acts model.txt, then receive a PDF report
Write model.txt with parameters and values, run pict model.txt, get every exhaustive combination
Write test scripts first, run pict on the scripts, then read a coverage percentage
Write model.txt with parameters and values, run pict model.txt, get a tab-separated test plan
Draw the model in a GUI, export it as XML, then run the IPOG algorithm by hand

explanation.en: PICT reads a simple text model file that defines parameters and values, is run from the command line with pict model.txt, and outputs an optimized, tab-separated test plan. It does not output every exhaustive combination; the point is a reduced suite.

prompt.en: In a browser/OS model, Safari only runs on macOS, so a test such as Safari + Windows cannot be executed. Which tool feature keeps such tests out of the generated suite?

en: Seeding
Constraints
Generating all exhaustive combinations
Raising the strength from 2-way to 3-way
Switching to 1-way smoke testing

explanation.en: Constraints such as IF [Browser] = "Safari" THEN [OS] = "macOS"; tell the tool which combinations are impossible or invalid, making the suite realistic and executable. Seeding does a different job: it forces specific tests into the suite.

prompt.en: In combinatorial testing tools, what is seeding?

en: Raising the strength t so that every trio of values is covered
Randomly sampling a subset of all exhaustive combinations
Removing tests that cover the same value pair more than once
Telling the tool which value combinations are impossible or invalid
Manually specifying test cases that must be included in the final suite

explanation.en: Seeding forces specific, pre-defined test cases, such as the most common user configuration or a previously known bug scenario, into the final suite. Declaring invalid combinations is what constraints do.

prompt.en: In the e-commerce payment case study, 1,296 full-combination test cases were reduced to about 25 pairwise tests. What outcome does the lecture report?

en: A 98% reduction in test cases with about 90% pairwise coverage
A 50% reduction in test cases with 98% pairwise coverage
A 98% reduction in test cases with 100% pairwise coverage
A 90% reduction in test cases with 100% pairwise coverage
A 75% reduction in test cases with full exhaustive coverage

explanation.en: Going from 1,296 to about 25 tests is a 98% reduction while still covering 100% of the value pairs. Pairwise testing does not keep exhaustive coverage; it guarantees full coverage of pairs.

prompt.en: Which task is a good fit for combinatorial testing as a primary technique?

en: API parameter testing of REST/SOAP endpoints
Security testing of a web application's login page
Testing complex user workflows with sequential steps
Performance testing of a high-traffic web service
Testing a state machine where the order of events matters

explanation.en: API parameter testing is listed with configuration/compatibility testing, complex form validation and systems with many independent parameters as good uses. Sequential workflows and order-dependent state machines are not primary uses, and for performance and security testing it is only a supplement, not a replacement.

prompt.en: What does the term "combinatorial explosion" refer to?

en: The failure of a test generator when two of its constraints contradict each other
Linear growth of test cases each time one new value is added to a parameter
The sharp drop in test cases achieved when moving from exhaustive to pairwise testing
The rapid rise in defects when many parameters interact in a production system
Exponential growth in test cases that makes exhaustive testing impossible

explanation.en: Combinatorial explosion is the exponential growth in the number of test cases as parameter values are combined (for example 5^10 = 9,765,625), which makes exhaustive testing impossible. The growth is exponential, not linear.

prompt.en: In the smart home lab, the PICT constraint IF [Security] = "Armed Away" THEN [Lighting] = "Off"; is added. What effect does it have on the generated tests?

en: Armed Away and Lighting = Off never appear in the same test
Every test with Security = Armed Away has Lighting = Off
Security = Armed Away is excluded from the suite entirely
Every test with Lighting = Off has Security = Armed Away
Lighting is set to Off in every test, whatever the Security value

explanation.en: The IF-THEN constraint marks Armed Away combined with any Lighting value other than Off as invalid, so every Armed Away test has Lighting = Off. It does not restrict other Security values, so Lighting = Off can still appear with Disarmed or Armed Home.

sets.title: Week 10: Security Testing & Threat Modeling (OWASP ZAP)

prompt.en: Which statement matches the IBM "Cost of a Data Breach Report 2023" figures presented in the lecture?

en: Breaches take on average 147 days to identify and contain
The average cost of a data breach is $4.45 billion
Healthcare is the most expensive sector, averaging $10.93 million per breach
Healthcare is the cheapest sector, averaging $4.45 million per breach
The average data breach costs $10.93 million across all industries

explanation.en: The report gives an average breach cost of $4.45 million, an average of 277 days to identify and contain a breach, and $10.93 million for healthcare, the most expensive industry. $10.93 million is the healthcare figure, not the overall average.

prompt.en: Which breach is correctly matched with its cause?

en: Equifax (2017): supply chain attack
SolarWinds (2020): unpatched Apache Struts vulnerability
Log4Shell (2021): unpatched Apache Struts vulnerability
Equifax (2017): remote code execution in a common logging library
SolarWinds (2020): supply chain attack

explanation.en: SolarWinds (2020) was a supply chain attack that compromised 18,000+ organizations. Equifax (2017) was caused by an unpatched Apache Struts vulnerability (147 million records lost), and Log4Shell (2021) by remote code execution in a common logging library.

prompt.en: What is the key message of the "old way vs. new way" comparison of security in the development lifecycle?

en: Security testing replaces the normal test phase once code is complete
Security is a continuous process integrated throughout the entire SDLC
Security testing is a separate phase performed just before release
Security is handled only in the Monitor stage after deployment
Security work starts only after a breach has been detected

explanation.en: The lecture states that security is not a phase but a continuous process integrated throughout the entire SDLC, with threat modeling, SAST and DAST built into the cycle. A single security-testing phase just before release is the crossed-out "old way".

prompt.en: In the lecture's "new way" lifecycle diagram, where are SAST and DAST placed?

en: DAST (dynamic analysis) at Code, SAST (static analysis) at Test
Both SAST and DAST in one security phase just before Release
SAST (static analysis) at Deploy, DAST (dynamic analysis) at Plan
SAST (static analysis) at Code, DAST (dynamic analysis) at Test
SAST (static analysis) at Plan, DAST (dynamic analysis) at Monitor

explanation.en: The diagram attaches SAST (Static Analysis) to the Code stage and DAST (Dynamic Analysis) to the Test stage, with threat modeling placed early, between Plan and Code. Grouping both into one pre-release phase is the "old way" the slide rejects.

prompt.en: Starting from "What are we building?", in which order does the threat modeling process ask its four questions?

en: What are we building? → What can go wrong? → What will we do about it? → Did we do a good job?
What are we building? → What will we do about it? → What can go wrong? → Did we do a good job?
What are we building? → What will we do about it? → Did we do a good job? → What can go wrong?
What are we building? → Did we do a good job? → What can go wrong? → What will we do about it?
What are we building? → What can go wrong? → Did we do a good job? → What will we do about it?

explanation.en: The cycle runs from system definition and analysis (What are we building?) to threat identification (What can go wrong?), then mitigation and countermeasures (What will we do about it?), and finally validation and verification (Did we do a good job?). Countermeasures can only be chosen after threats have been identified.

prompt.en: What do the six letters of STRIDE stand for?

en: Scanning, Tampering, Replay, Interception, Discoverability, Elevation of Privilege
Spoofing, Tampering, Reproducibility, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Exploitability
Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege
Sniffing, Tampering, Repudiation, Injection, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege
Spoofing, Tracing, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Damage, Elevation of Privilege

explanation.en: STRIDE names six threat categories: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service and Elevation of Privilege. Damage, Reproducibility, Exploitability and Discoverability are DREAD factors used for risk scoring, not STRIDE categories.

prompt.en: During threat modeling, a team notes that a standard user could find a way to gain admin access. Which STRIDE category does this threat belong to?

en: Information Disclosure
Elevation of Privilege
Repudiation
Tampering
Spoofing

explanation.en: A standard user gaining admin access is the lecture's example of Elevation of Privilege. Spoofing is illustrated by a fake login page, Tampering by SQL injection, Repudiation by deleting audit logs and Information Disclosure by sensitive data in an error message.

prompt.en: How do STRIDE and DREAD differ in threat modeling?

en: STRIDE sorts threats into six categories; DREAD quantifies each threat's risk
DREAD sorts threats into six categories; STRIDE quantifies each threat's risk
STRIDE lists the OWASP Top 10 risks; DREAD lists the fixes for them
STRIDE is a SAST tool used at Code; DREAD is a DAST tool used at Test
STRIDE is ZAP's active scan mode; DREAD is ZAP's passive scan mode

explanation.en: STRIDE provides six categories of threats to guide the analysis, while DREAD rates a threat on five factors and averages them into a risk score, because not all threats are equal. Neither is a scanner mode or a list of OWASP risks.

prompt.en: A threat is rated Damage 6, Reproducibility 5, Exploitability 7, Affected Users 4 and Discoverability 8. Using the DREAD calculation from the lecture, what is its risk score?

explanation.en: The DREAD score is the average of the five ratings: (6 + 5 + 7 + 4 + 8) / 5 = 30 / 5 = 6.0. 30 is the sum before dividing, and 8.4 is the score of the lecture's SQL injection example.

prompt.en: Which OWASP Top 10 code and category pairing is correct?

en: A01: Injection
A02: Security Misconfiguration
A03: Cryptographic Failures
A05: Vulnerable and Outdated Components
A01: Broken Access Control

explanation.en: In the OWASP Top 10 list shown, A01 is Broken Access Control, A02 Cryptographic Failures, A03 Injection, A05 Security Misconfiguration and A06 Vulnerable and Outdated Components.

prompt.en:
Which change fixes the SQL injection in this code?
query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = '" + user_input + "';"
cursor.execute(query)

en: Replace SELECT * with SELECT username so that fewer columns are returned
Check that the logged-in user's ID matches the requested resource ID
Run a ZAP passive scan before each query to filter out malicious input
Append user_input after the closing quote instead of inside the quotes
Use a ? placeholder and pass user_input as a separate argument to execute()

explanation.en: The secure code uses "SELECT * FROM users WHERE username = ?;" with cursor.execute(query, (user_input,)), so input such as ' OR '1'='1 is no longer concatenated into the SQL string. Checking the user's ID against the resource ID is the fix for IDOR, not for injection.

prompt.en: A logged-in user calls GET /api/user/123 for their own data, changes the URL to GET /api/user/124 and receives another user's data. What fix does the lecture recommend?

en: Use parameterized queries with ? placeholders in every API endpoint
Encrypt the API response so that other users' data cannot be read
On the server, check that the user's ID matches the requested resource ID
Run ZAP's active scan in production so that such requests are blocked
On the client, check that the ID in the URL belongs to the current user

explanation.en: This is an IDOR flaw (A01: Broken Access Control); the fix is a server-side check that the logged-in user's ID matches the requested resource ID before any data is returned. Parameterized queries fix SQL injection, not access control.

prompt.en: Which OWASP ZAP feature is used for automated site mapping?

en: HTML report
Spider
Active scan
Intercepting proxy
Passive scan

explanation.en: The lecture lists "Spider for Automated Site Mapping" among ZAP's features. The passive scan monitors traffic and the active scan sends attack payloads to find vulnerabilities; neither is the mapping feature.

prompt.en: A tester with explicit permission wants ZAP to find SQL injection, cross-site scripting (XSS) and path traversal flaws in a test system. Which ZAP capability is designed for this?

en: Active scan
Spider
Intercepting proxy
Passive scan
Report generation

explanation.en: The active scan ("the attacker") sends thousands of malicious payloads and finds critical flaws such as SQL injection, XSS and path traversal. The passive scan only monitors traffic and finds low-hanging fruit such as missing security headers.

prompt.en: Which statement about ZAP's passive scan is correct?

en: It sends thousands of malicious payloads to find vulnerabilities
It modifies requests in transit to trigger cross-site scripting errors
It maps the whole site automatically without observing any traffic
It only monitors HTTP traffic and is safe to use on production systems
It finds critical flaws such as SQL injection by attacking input fields

explanation.en: The passive scan ("the listener") monitors HTTP traffic without modifying it, finds issues like missing security headers, sensitive info in comments and insecure cookie flags, and is safe on production systems. Sending malicious payloads to find SQL injection is what the active scan does.

prompt.en: In the OWASP Juice Shop lab (http://localhost:3000), what is the first, reconnaissance step of the mission?

en: Run the active scanner to find SQL injection on the login page
Enter <script>alert('XSS')</script> into the site's search bar
Score every discovered page with the DREAD formula
Generate the ZAP HTML report and send it to the developers
Browse the site through ZAP's proxy and perform a passive scan

explanation.en: Reconnaissance means using ZAP's proxy to browse the site and perform a passive scan. Using the active scanner for SQL injection on the login page and testing reflected XSS in the search bar are the later exploitation steps.

prompt.en: In a professional ZAP vulnerability report, what does the "Evidence" shown with the affected URL contain?

en: The DREAD score of the finding
The specific attack payload
The count of High, Medium and Low risks
The recommended code fix
The CWE reference for the weakness

explanation.en: The report pairs the affected URL with evidence, which is the specific attack payload (for example the <script>alert('XSS')</script> request). CWE links belong under References, risk counts under the Risk Breakdown, and fixes under Solution Recommendations.

prompt.en: Which rule for security testing does the lecture state?

en: Always get explicit, written permission and respect the agreed-upon scope
Systems outside the scope may be tested if they look clearly vulnerable
Permission is needed only for active scans run against production systems
Verbal permission is enough as long as the scope is put in writing later
Written permission is needed only once a vulnerability has been found

explanation.en: The lecture says to ALWAYS get explicit, written permission before any testing, ALWAYS define and respect the agreed-upon scope, and NEVER test systems outside it, because unauthorized security testing is a crime. Permission is required before any testing, not only before active scans.

prompt.en: Which legal references does the lecture cite for unauthorized security testing?

en: Turkey: TCK Articles 343 and 344; USA: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)
Turkey: TCK Articles 234 and 235; USA: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)
Turkey: TCK Articles 243 and 244; USA: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA)
Turkey: TCK Articles 243 and 244; USA: Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE)
Turkey: TCK Articles 243 and 244; USA: OWASP Top 10 compliance rules

explanation.en: The lecture cites TCK Article 243 (Unauthorized Access) and Article 244 (System Disruption) for Turkey, and the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA) for the USA. CWE and the OWASP Top 10 are vulnerability references, not laws.

sets.title: Week 11: Chaos Engineering and Resilience Testing

prompt.en: In July 2024, a single software failure at CrowdStrike cost Fortune 500 companies an estimated how much in a matter of hours?

en: $540 million
$5.4 billion
$54 billion
$12.5 billion
$1.8 billion

explanation.en: The lecture cites an estimated $5.4 billion loss for Fortune 500 companies, showing that failures of complex distributed systems are a multi-billion dollar reality that traditional testing cannot anticipate.

prompt.en: According to the lecture, human error contributes to what share of preventable incidents?

explanation.en: The Hurricane Sandy slide states that human error contributes to 79% of preventable incidents; 43.3% is Amazon's reported decrease in SLA violations after GameDays.

prompt.en: Which sequence matches the timeline of Netflix's chaos engineering origin story?

en: 2008 database corruption, 2010 Chaos Monkey open-sourced, 2011 Simian Army announced, 2012 Chaos Kong created
2008 Chaos Monkey created, 2010 database corruption, 2011 Simian Army announced, 2012 open-sourced
2008 database corruption, 2010 Simian Army announced, 2011 Chaos Monkey created, 2012 open-sourced
2008 database corruption, 2010 Chaos Monkey created, 2011 Simian Army announced, 2012 open-sourced
2006 database corruption, 2008 Chaos Monkey created, 2010 Simian Army announced, 2012 open-sourced

explanation.en: After the August 2008 database corruption halted DVD shipping for three days, Netflix created Chaos Monkey in 2010, announced the Simian Army in 2011 and open-sourced it in 2012.

prompt.en: Which Simian Army tool simulates the failure of an entire AWS Availability Zone?

en: Chaos Gorilla
Latency Monkey
Chaos Kong
Security Monkey
Chaos Monkey

explanation.en: Chaos Gorilla simulates the loss of a whole AWS Availability Zone; Chaos Kong goes a step further and simulates a full AWS region failure.

prompt.en: A team wants to check that its services stay resilient when network communication becomes slow rather than failing outright. Which Simian Army tool is designed for this?

en: Chaos Monkey
Chaos Kong
Latency Monkey
Chaos Gorilla
Security Monkey

explanation.en: Latency Monkey injects artificial delays to test resilience to network degradation; Chaos Monkey instead randomly terminates production instances to test survival of instance loss.

prompt.en: How does principlesofchaos.org define Chaos Engineering?

en: Randomly breaking production systems without any hypothesis to see how users are affected
Experimenting on a system to build confidence that it can withstand turbulent conditions in production
Load testing a system to find the maximum traffic it can handle before it crashes in production
Testing a system before release to prove that it contains no defects under turbulent conditions
Simulating attacks on a system to find security vulnerabilities before they reach production

explanation.en: The quoted definition is experimenting on a system to build confidence in its capability to withstand turbulent conditions in production; the lecture also describes it as a hypothesis-driven, scientific practice.

prompt.en: In the fourth and final step of a chaos experiment, "Disprove Hypothesis", what do engineers do?

en: Inject real-world failure events such as server crashes, network partitions and CPU spikes
Restore every terminated instance and confirm that the hypothesis has been proven true
Predict that the steady state will continue in both the control and experimental groups
Systematically look for differences between the control and experimental groups to find weaknesses
Establish a measurable baseline of normal system behavior before anything is changed

explanation.en: Disproving the hypothesis means searching for differences between the control and experimental groups to expose weaknesses; defining a baseline, predicting that steady state continues and injecting failures are steps 1, 2 and 3.

prompt.en: In the lecture's payment-microservice example, which statement is the steady state hypothesis?

en: Inject real-world failure events into the checkout service and then record its error rate
Terminate 30% of the checkout service instances while the service is handling normal load
The checkout service must never fail, no matter how many of its instances are terminated
Auto-scaling and load balancing restore the checkout service within 30 seconds of the failure
Under normal load, the checkout service keeps p99 latency under 200ms and an error rate below 0.1%

explanation.en: A steady state hypothesis is a measurable, quantifiable description of normal behavior (p99 latency under 200ms, error rate below 0.1%); terminating 30% of instances is the experiment, and recovery within 30 seconds is the expected result.

prompt.en: A team is ready to run its first chaos experiment in production. Following the principle of minimizing the blast radius, which target should it start with?

en: An entire service
A full AWS region
A single container
Every pod in the cluster
One Availability Zone

explanation.en: The blast radius grows from container to instance/pod, service, Availability Zone and region, and teams should begin with the smallest possible blast radius in production, so a single container comes first.

prompt.en: What is the purpose of automated stop conditions (circuit breakers) in chaos experiments?

en: To halt an experiment if the system deviates too far from steady state
To widen the blast radius automatically after each successful run
To measure how long the system runs before its next failure occurs
To move an experiment from production back into a staging environment
To randomly terminate production instances during an experiment

explanation.en: Circuit breakers are a control mechanism for the blast radius: they automatically stop an experiment when the system strays too far from its steady state.

prompt.en: Which statement about the modern chaos engineering toolkit (2023-2025) is correct?

en: LitmusChaos is a CNCF project best suited to Kubernetes environments
AWS FIS is an open-source tool known as the original chaos tool
Chaos Monkey is a commercial SaaS tool aimed at enterprise adoption
Gremlin is a CNCF project with native Kubernetes (K8s) integration
Azure Chaos Studio is a commercial SaaS tool known for GameDays

explanation.en: LitmusChaos is the CNCF project with native K8s integration; Gremlin is the commercial SaaS tool known for being user-friendly and for GameDays, while Chaos Monkey is the original open-source tool.

prompt.en: A service runs on average 200 hours before it fails and then takes on average 2 hours to restore. Using the formula from the lecture, what is its MTBF?

en: 100 hours
200 hours
400 hours
198 hours
202 hours

explanation.en: MTBF = MTTF + MTTR, so 200 hours + 2 hours = 202 hours; 200 hours on its own is only the MTTF.

prompt.en: Which resilience metric answers the question "How long can a system be expected to run before it fails?"

en: p99 latency
MTTF (Mean Time to Failure)
MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures)
Error rate
MTTR (Mean Time to Recovery)

explanation.en: MTTF measures how long a system runs before it fails; MTTR measures how quickly service is restored after a failure, and MTBF is the total time from one failure to the next.

prompt.en: According to the industry benchmark for MTTR given in the lecture, elite teams restore service in under how much time?

en: 60 minutes
30 minutes
5 minutes
30 seconds
15 minutes

explanation.en: The benchmark is under 30 minutes for top teams and under 5 minutes for elite teams.

prompt.en: A system offering 99.99% availability ("four nines") allows approximately how much downtime per year?

en: 5.26 minutes
8.76 hours
44 minutes
52.56 minutes
4.4 minutes

explanation.en: Four nines means 52.56 minutes of annual downtime (about 4.4 minutes per month); 8.76 hours per year corresponds to three nines and 5.26 minutes to five nines.

prompt.en: What key result did Amazon report after implementing GameDays?

en: A 43.3% decrease in mean time to recovery
A 79% decrease in preventable incidents
A 50% decrease in deployment failures
A 43.3% decrease in SLA violations
A 30% decrease in p99 latency

explanation.en: Amazon's dedicated 2-4 hour GameDay periods led to a 43.3% decrease in SLA violations; 79% is the share of preventable incidents attributed to human error.

prompt.en: What distinguishes Google's DiRT (Disaster Recovery Testing) program from the other industry approaches described in the lecture?

en: It randomly terminates production instances to test instance loss
It provides native Kubernetes integration as a CNCF project
It runs automated chaos experiments continuously in production
It sets aside dedicated 2-4 hour periods for teams to run experiments
It goes beyond technology to test business processes and human response

explanation.en: DiRT, founded in 2006 by Site Reliability Engineers, also tests business processes and human response; continuous automated chaos in production describes Netflix, and 2-4 hour periods describe Amazon's GameDays.

prompt.en: In the Honeycomb case study on an AWS Availability Zone failure, when did the team intentionally run its production experiment?

en: Only after a real AZ outage, to confirm the cause
During a maintenance window, with users logged out
During peak traffic, for a realistic test
Before any staging tests, to save rollout time
During off-peak hours, to avoid customer impact

explanation.en: Honeycomb ran staging tests first, then progressed to production and intentionally ran the experiment during peak traffic for a realistic test, terminating a third of its 'Shepherd' pods with zero customer impact.

prompt.en: Which statement reflects the core principles of resilient engineering presented in the lecture?

en: Reducing MTTR is often more valuable than trying to prevent all failures
Experiments should stay manual and separate from the CI/CD pipeline
Preventing all failures is more valuable than reducing recovery time
Experiments should start with the largest blast radius to learn the most
Technical tools alone are enough; no cultural change is required

explanation.en: The lecture states that reducing MTTR is often more valuable than trying to prevent all failures; it also says to start with a small blast radius, pair tools with cultural transformation and automate experiments in CI/CD.

sets.title: Week 12: CI/CD Pipelines and Docker for Testing

prompt.en: In the lecture, Docker is introduced as the tool that solves which universal problem?

en: The 'it works on my machine' problem
The 'slow code review' problem
The 'merge conflicts on main' problem
The 'too many manual releases' problem
The 'flaky end-to-end tests' problem

explanation.en: Docker solves the 'it works on my machine' problem by ensuring consistency everywhere, while CI/CD pipelines are described as the engine for automating software delivery.

prompt.en: A team's pipeline automatically packages every successfully tested build and delivers it to a staging environment, but a person must approve each release to production. Which practice is this?

en: Continuous Deployment
Smoke testing
Infrastructure as Code
Continuous Integration
Continuous Delivery

explanation.en: Continuous Delivery extends CI by delivering tested builds to staging and keeps a manual gate before production; Continuous Deployment removes that gate and deploys every passing change to production without human intervention.

prompt.en: What is the stated goal of Continuous Integration (CI)?

en: Validate the full system in a production-like staging environment
Perform a basic health check right after each deployment
Automatically deploy every passing change directly to production
Find and fix integration bugs early and quickly through frequent commits
Keep code deployable at all times, with a manual gate before production

explanation.en: In CI developers commit frequently and each commit triggers a build and tests, with the goal of finding integration bugs early; keeping code deployable behind a manual gate is the goal of Continuous Delivery.

prompt.en: Which order matches the stages of a CI/CD pipeline?

en: Build → Source → Test → Deploy → Staging
Source → Build → Test → Staging → Deploy
Test → Source → Build → Staging → Deploy
Source → Test → Build → Staging → Deploy
Source → Build → Staging → Test → Deploy

explanation.en: Code is committed to version control (Source), compiled or packaged (Build), validated by automated tests (Test), deployed to pre-production for final validation (Staging) and then released to users (Deploy).

prompt.en: In the test pyramid used for pipeline testing, what is the approximate distribution of tests?

en: Unit ~33%, Integration ~33%, E2E ~33%
Unit ~10%, Integration ~20%, E2E ~70%
Unit ~70%, Integration ~20%, E2E ~10%
Unit ~20%, Integration ~70%, E2E ~10%
Unit ~50%, Integration ~30%, E2E ~20%

explanation.en: Unit tests form the wide base (~70%, fast and cheap, run first), integration tests the middle (~20%) and E2E tests the small top (~10%, slow and expensive but highest confidence).

prompt.en: A new release has just been deployed and the team wants a basic health check to confirm it is working. Which test type does the pipeline testing table assign to this Deploy stage?

en: E2E tests
Linting and static analysis
Integration tests
Smoke tests
Unit tests

explanation.en: Smoke tests run at the Deploy stage as a basic health check after deployment; E2E tests belong to the Staging stage, where the full system is validated in a production-like environment.

prompt.en: Which benefit of Docker for testing refers to running tests in a clean, pristine environment every time, eliminating interference?

en: Fail Fast
Consistency
Isolation
Scalability
Caching

explanation.en: Isolation gives every test run a clean environment; Consistency means identical environments for development, testing and production, and Scalability means spinning up containers on demand for parallel tests.

prompt.en: Which statement correctly compares containers with virtual machines?

en: Containers share the host kernel, while each VM runs a full guest OS
Containers carry hypervisor overhead, while VMs run at near-native speed
Containers give hardware-level isolation, VMs process-level isolation
Containers are gigabytes in size, while VMs are only megabytes
Containers start in minutes, while VMs start in a few seconds

explanation.en: Containers share the host kernel, start in seconds, are megabytes in size, run at near-native speed and isolate at process level; VMs run a full guest OS on a hypervisor, start in minutes, are gigabytes in size and isolate at hardware level.

prompt.en: In Docker terminology, what is an image?

en: A tool for defining and running multi-container applications
A runnable, isolated instance created from a read-only template
A text file with instructions for building the application package
A public registry for storing and sharing application packages
A read-only template containing the application and its environment

explanation.en: An image is a read-only template (the 'class definition' or blueprint); a container is a runnable, isolated instance of it, a Dockerfile is the recipe that builds it and Docker Hub is the registry that stores and shares it.

prompt.en: A tester needs to start a web application, its database and a cache together as one multi-container setup. Which Docker concept is designed for this?

en: docker exec
Docker Compose
Docker image
Dockerfile
Docker Hub

explanation.en: Docker Compose is the tool for defining and running multi-container applications (the 'orchestra conductor' for your services); a Dockerfile only holds the instructions to build one image.

prompt.en: After installing Docker, which command runs a built-in container whose successful run confirms that the installation is complete?

en: docker pull nginx
docker --version
docker build -t hello-world .
docker ps -a
docker run hello-world

explanation.en: The second verification step, docker run hello-world, runs the built-in "hello-world" container; docker --version only checks which Docker version is installed.

prompt.en: Which Docker command lists all containers, both running and stopped?

en: docker rmi
docker images
docker ps -a
docker ps
docker logs -f

explanation.en: docker ps -a lists all containers whether running or stopped; plain docker ps lists only running containers, and docker images lists local images.

prompt.en: In the Python test Dockerfile, why are requirements.txt copied and the dependencies installed before the rest of the application code is copied?

en: To make the final image read-only before the tests start
For better caching of the dependency installation step
Because COPY . . would otherwise delete installed packages
So that pytest runs automatically while the image is built
Because WORKDIR can only be set after pip has finished

explanation.en: The Dockerfile comment says dependencies are copied and installed first for better caching; the rest of the code is copied afterwards with COPY . .

prompt.en: What does the instruction CMD ["pytest", "-v", "--html=report.html"] do in the Python test Dockerfile?

en: Selects the lightweight base image to start from
Installs pytest and the other listed dependencies
Runs pytest once while the image is being built
Defines the command that runs when the container starts
Sets the working directory inside the container

explanation.en: CMD defines the command to run when the container starts, so docker run my-python-tests executes pytest; RUN pip install installs the dependencies, WORKDIR sets the directory and FROM picks the base image.

prompt.en: Which statement about Jenkins, GitLab CI and GitHub Actions is correct?

en: Jenkins is self-hosted and highly configurable, with a steeper learning curve
Jenkins is built into GitHub and is best suited to open-source projects
GitHub Actions is best for complex enterprise needs and maximum control
GitHub Actions is self-hosted and configured with a Groovy Jenkinsfile
GitLab CI supports Docker only through plugins and is the easiest to learn

explanation.en: Jenkins is self-hosted, highly configurable, supports Docker via plugins and has the steeper learning curve, suiting complex enterprise needs; GitHub Actions is built into GitHub, is the easiest to learn and suits GitHub-hosted and open-source projects.

prompt.en: A project is hosted on GitLab and will use GitLab CI. Which file defines its pipeline configuration?

en: .gitlab-ci.yml
.gitlab/workflows/ci.yml
Dockerfile
.github/workflows/*.yml
Jenkinsfile

explanation.en: GitLab CI is configured with .gitlab-ci.yml; Jenkins uses a Groovy-based Jenkinsfile and GitHub Actions uses YAML files under .github/workflows/.

prompt.en: In a GitHub Actions workflow file, which key specifies the virtual machine environment for a job (for example ubuntu-latest)?

en: steps
uses
runs-on
on
services

explanation.en: runs-on selects the virtual machine environment for the job; on defines the triggering event, services spins up other containers such as a database, and steps lists the sequence of tasks.

prompt.en: A team reorders its pipeline so that the quickest checks, unit tests and linting, run before the slower test suites. Which best practice is this?

en: Environment Consistency
Parallelize
Monitor Metrics
Cache Dependencies
Fail Fast

explanation.en: Fail Fast means running the quickest tests (unit, linting) first; Parallelize means running multiple test suites simultaneously using matrix builds or test sharding.

prompt.en: What outcome did Etsy achieve after adopting robust CI/CD pipelines, Infrastructure as Code and fully integrated automated testing?

en: It grew from a few deployments per day to 50+ deploys per hour
It grew from a few deployments per year to 50+ deploys per day
It cut deployments to one per quarter in order to reach zero downtime
It grew from one deployment per week to thousands of deploys per day
It grew from a few deployments per month to 5+ deploys per day

explanation.en: Etsy went from a few deployments per year to 50+ deploys per day with near-zero downtime and faster bug detection; 'thousands of code changes daily' describes Netflix.

sets.title: Week 13: Formal Verification: Bridging Proofs and Testing

prompt.en: Which statement expresses the fundamental insight of the lecture about testing and formal verification?

en: Testing proves correctness; formal verification estimates how often bugs occur
Testing proves the absence of bugs; formal verification shows their presence
Testing and formal verification both prove the absence of all possible bugs
Testing finds design flaws; formal verification finds only coding errors
Testing shows the presence of bugs; formal verification proves their absence

explanation.en: Testing runs a finite set of inputs, so it can reveal bugs but not rule them out, while formal verification constructs a mathematical proof that they are absent. The reversed statement swaps the two roles.

prompt.en: Exhaustively testing a 64-bit processor requires 2^64 (about 18 quintillion) test cases. At 1 billion tests per second, approximately how long does the lecture say this would take?

en: About 635 years
About 18 years
About 64 years
About 6,350 years
About 2,048 years

explanation.en: The state space explosion example states that 2^64 test cases at 1 billion tests per second would take approximately 635 years, which is why exhaustive testing is infeasible.

prompt.en: In the argument for why testing isn't enough, what does the "needle in a haystack" problem refer to?

en: Static analysis tools report many bugs that turn out not to be real
Proof assistants need a human to guide every step of a proof
Properties must be written in temporal logic before they can be checked
Critical bugs lurk in rare combinations of concurrent events and timing conditions
The number of test cases grows exponentially with the size of the input

explanation.en: The needle-in-a-haystack problem is about rarity: critical bugs hide in rare combinations of concurrent events, fault scenarios and timing conditions, and at millions of requests per second such "extremely rare" events happen regularly. Exponential growth of test cases is the separate state space explosion problem.

prompt.en: Which statement correctly contrasts testing and formal verification?

en: Testing constructs a mathematical proof; formal verification runs a finite set of inputs
Testing covers only the tested cases; formal verification covers all possible inputs and states
Testing can prove the absence of bugs; formal verification can only prove their presence
Testing covers all possible inputs and states; formal verification covers only the proven cases
Testing covers design and implementation; formal verification focuses only on the implementation
